exhibited:
Goldsmiths' Company, London,
Treasures of the English Church, 30 May 2008.
catalogue_note: Penelope Taylor (née Lechmere) was the daughter of Nicholas Lechmere of Hanley Castle. She married in 1664, the son of the wealthy landowner, Ralph Taylor. The Taylor family lived at Welland Court, near St James' church, until the mid-1750s. The present cup was one of two pieces presented to the church by the Taylor family, the other being a silver-gilt-mounted stoneware jug, hallmarked for London, 1582 (see Bonhams, London, 23 November 2011, lot 195). Both pieces were sold by the church in 2011 to raise funds for its renovation.

title: A German parcel-gilt silver tankard, Philipp Küsel, Augsburg, 1691-1695
description:
the base chased and embossed with fruit, the body with Roman emperors between fruit and leaves and a coat-of-arms and the inscription 'ERMAN OTTO GRAFF ZU LIMBOURG UND BRONCHORST. HERR ZU STYRUM. WISCH BORCKELDE UND GEHMEN. ERBANNER HERR DES FÜRSTENTHUMBS GELDEREN UND GRAFFSCHAFFT ZUTPHEN DER RÖM. KAÿ MAÿ WÜRCKLICHER CAMERHERR. V. obrister', dated 1678, the scroll handle with a demi-putto, the hinged cover with a ball finial, engraved under the base 'WD, PTD, ASH' and dated 1748, marked on the body and cover with town and maker's mark

description_en:
the base chased and embossed with fruit, the body with Roman emperors between fruit and leaves and a coat-of-arms and the inscription 'ERMAN OTTO GRAFF ZU LIMBOURG UND BRONCHORST. HERR ZU STYRUM. WISCH BORCKELDE UND GEHMEN. ERBANNER HERR DES FÜRSTENTHUMBS GELDEREN UND GRAFFSCHAFFT ZUTPHEN DER RÖM. KAÿ MAÿ WÜRCKLICHER CAMERHERR. V. obrister', dated 1678, the scroll handle with a demi-putto, the hinged cover with a ball finial, engraved under the base 'WD, PTD, ASH' and dated 1748, marked on the body and cover with town and maker's mark

23.5cm, 9¼in. high
652gr., 21oz
provenance:
Of Royal and Noble Descent,
Sotheby's Londres, 23 janvier 2014, lot 123.
catalogue_note:
The arms are those of Counts Limburg-Stirum.
Field Marshall Count Hermann Otto II , of Limburg Stirum and Bronckhorst. (1646 - 1704) became commander of an Imperial regiment (
Obrister of his Roman Imperial Majesty) in 1678, the date engraved on the tankard. The images of Roman emperors are fitting for a military servant of the Emperor, and coincide with his promotion in 1696 to the rank of Field Marshall. In 1704, he led the Duke of Marlborough's assault at the Battle of Schellenberg (also known as the Battle of Donauwörth) during the War of the Spanish Succession where he was mortally wounded.

catalogue_note:
This impressive cup depicts the famous Battle of Vienna fought between the Austrians and the Turks in 1683. Since July, the Ottoman army, led by Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa, had been attempting to capture the imperial city. Ultimately, the imperial forces and their allies launched a final assault on September 12, defeating the Grand Vizier. The lid of our cup features Zeus—accompanied by his eagle—striking down the turbaned Ottomans.

Legend says the first croissants were created during this siege. Bakers working through the night reportedly heard the Ottomans attempting to tunnel beneath the city walls to invade. Thanks to their intervention, the tunnels were destroyed; following the Austrian victory, and to commemorate the battle, the bakers are said to have created a pastry shaped like the Ottoman crescent—symbolically "devouring" the enemy.

description_en:
After Adriaen de Vries (circa 1556 - 1626), model probably Augsburg, circa 1597, cast Southern-German, probably Augsburg, mid-17th century
Venus or Nymph washing her foot

bronze; on a later limestone socle
bronze: 40cm., 15¾in.
46cm., 18⅛in. overall
literature:
J. Menzhausen, W. Klonke,
Einführung in das Grüne Gewölbe, Altenbourg, 1977, pp. 58-59, ill. p. 59;
D. Syndram,
Das Grüne Gewölbe zu Dresden. Führer durch seine Geschichte und seine Sammlungen, Munich / Berlin 1994, pp. 70-72, ill. p. 72;
U. Berger, V. Krahn,
Bronzen der Renaissance und des Barock: Katalog der Sammlung, Sammlungskataloge des Herzog Anton Ulrich-Museums, Brunswick, 1994, p. 241.
L. O. Larsson,
Adriaen de Vries, Adrianvs Fries Hagiensis Batavvs 1545 – 1626, Vienna / Munich, 1964, fig. 60; C. List,
Kleinbronzen Europas, vom Mittelalter bis zur Gegenwart, Munich, 1983, pp. 158-159; F. Scholten (ed.),
Adriaen de Vries 1556 – 1626, exh. cat. Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, December 1998 – March 1999, Nationalmuseum, Stockholm, April– August 1999, The J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles, October 1999 - January 2000, pp. 131-133.
catalogue_note:
The composition of this young woman at her toilette derives from a Hellenistic prototype, known through a Roman copy of the 2nd century AD preserved in Florence (Uffizi Gallery, inv. 1914, no. 19), of which the Paduan Giovanni Paolo Fonduli da Crema (active 1468 - 1484) cast the first bronze reduction (c. 1480 - 1490; Wallace Collection, inv. S72). The distinctly Mannerist torsion of the body in the present
Nymph, as well as the movement of her right hand reaching towards her raised left foot, also echoes Giambologna’s marble
Bathsheba, executed c. 1571 - 1573 and sometimes also described as a
Female Figure or
Venus
(J. Paul Getty Museum, inv. 82.SA.37). The Florentine master devoted a significant part of his oeuvre to the theme of the toilette, in which the subject depicted often seems to serve little more than as a pretext for the representation of the female nude.
Adriaen de Vries, to whom the present model is now attributed, may have seen Giambologna’s
Bathsheba in Florence between 1581 and 1586, or, more probably, in Munich, in the collections of the Duke of Bavaria, to whom it had been presented by Francesco de’ Medici. Indeed, the detail of the braid falling along the
Nymph’s right shoulder is probably a direct quotation from Giambologna’s marble. The composition, rooted in the Florentine tradition, also recalls the seated figures precariously balanced on the basin of the
Fountain of Neptune by Bartolomeo Ammannati (1511 - 1592), executed c. 1560 - 1574 (Piazza della Signoria, Florence).
Only two other examples of the present model are known: a bronze in Brunswick, described as
Venus or
Nymph Washing Her Foot
(Herzog Anton Ulrich-Museum, inv. Bro 93; H. 40.3 cm), and a lead version in London, of lesser quality and depicting the female figure seated on a bench (Victoria and Albert Museum, inv. A.2-1946; H. 42 cm). According to C. List, the Munich painter Johann Matthias Kager (1575–1634), who had been based in Augsburg since 1602, depicted this model in a drawing dated 1615 (see op. cit., p. 159; whereabout unknown). This document attests to the circulation of the model as early as the first quarter of the 17 th century.
Originally from The Hague, Adriaen de Vries was the sculptor of choice of the great courts of northern Europe. He is documented in Giambologna’s workshop in Florence from 1581, where he absorbed Mannerist principles and mastered the art of bronze casting. After a period in Milan with Pompeo Leoni, he worked for Charles Emmanuel I, Duke of Savoy, in Turin, before moving to Prague, where he entered the service of Rudolf II from 1593 onwards. Alongside his duties at the imperial court, he executed important commissions in Augsburg, notably the
Mercury and
Hercules fountains, and continued to work for Christian IV of Denmark and Albrecht von Wallenstein. Adriaen de Vries was a key figure in the artistic exchanges between Florence and the rest of Europe, particularly in the dissemination of Florentine Mannerism in northern Europe.
A parallel may be drawn between the present
Nymph, with its contorted body, and the two allegorical figures flanking the bronze bust of
Christian II of Saxony, cast by de Vries around 1603 (Staatliche Kunstsammlungen, Skulpturensammlung, Dresden, inv. H4 001 / 004). It bears an even closer resemblance to one of the figures from the
Fountain of Hercules in Augsburg, made between 1597 and 1602. Indeed, it is now generally accepted that it was probably cast from a preparatory study for the Augsburg figure (see F. Scholten, op. cit., pp. 131–132).
An analysis of the composition of the present bronze indicates that the alloy used corresponds to that of the Brunswick statuette. Small points visible on the surface of both bronzes also reveal a comparable arrangement of the metal structure used to hold the core in place during casting. These visual and technical similarities suggest that the two bronzes were probably cast in the same Southern German foundry.

catalogue_note:
Johann Eissler became master in 1640 and specialised in mounted objects, particularly those featuring ivory. While no specific casket has been attributed to him, this type of decoration is known in the work of other goldsmiths such as Jonas Laminit or Balthasar Gelb (see H. Seling,
Die Kunst der Augsburger Goldschmiede, 1529–1868, Munich, 1980, illus. 551 and 552).
The rock crystal engraving can be attributed to Hermann Schwinger (1640–1683), likely a pupil of Georg Schwanhardt (1601–1657). Schwanhardt had trained under Caspar Lehman, engraver to Emperor Rudolf II in Prague, and secured the imperial license following his master's death. He subsequently established a school of engravers, of which Schwinger was a member; the school's style is characterized by delicate miniature landscapes framed by bold scrolling foliage.

description_en:

agate, in an enamelled pendant mount

literature:
P. Malgouyres,
Pierres gravées : Camées, intailles et bagues de la collection Guy Ladrière, Paris, 2022, p. 99-100
catalogue_note:
This finely carved cameo depicting Jupiter full frontal is inspired by ancient gems representing the king of the gods. Although a frontal image of the god, it recalls the famous
Cameo Zulian which shows the god in three quarter profile.
The
Cameo Zulian, which was one of the most celebrated gems in the 18th century, was discovered in Ephesus around 1787, before being acquired by Luca Cortazzi, who gifted it to Girolamo Zulian, the Venetian representative in Constantinople; it is today the Museo Archeologico Nazionale in Venice. The present cameo perhaps owes its inspiration to the oak-wreathed representation of Jupiter, cut in chrysoprase, in the Penn Museum (inv. no. 29-128-1501). The Penn cameo was once owned by Maxwell Sommerville, who considered it to be ancient; it is today thought to date to the first half of the 19th century. Probably the most famous cameo depicting Jupiter (full figure) is the
Camée de Chartres in the Bibliothèque nationale in Paris; a masterpiece of Imperial gem engraving once owned by Charles V of France (Bnf, inv. no. Camée. 1).
For late Neoclassical cameos representing similar subjects, compare with the
Cameo with the head of Helios-Serapide by Giuseppe Girometti (1780-1851) in the Musei Vaticani, Rome (inv. no. 66660; acquired by Gregory XVI in 1845).

catalogue_note: This beautifully carved cameo depicts a Roman triumph. Given the inclusion of elephants, the general might be identified with Manius Curius Dentatus (died 270 BC) or Pompey the Great (106 - 48 BC) both of whose triumphs featured elephants. Interestingly, a Renaissance cameo in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London, includes elephants (inv. no. A.34-1937). The style of the carving of the present cameo indicates that it was made in the early to mid-19 th century; compare with a cameo with Jupiter sold at Sotheby's London on 9 July 2020, lot 62.

catalogue_note: Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden (1594–1632) is known as the "Lion of the North." It was under his reign that Sweden became a strong and prosperous European power. He is considered one of the greatest strategists of his time, having achieved frequent victories during the battles of the Thirty Years' War. He implemented economic and agrarian reforms that fostered his country's development. Through his military actions, he maintained a political and religious balance between Catholics and Protestants in Europe. Tragically, he died at the Battle of Lützen in 1632; he was one of the few monarchs to lead his troops in combat, following the example of his role model, Alexander the Great.

description:
on three ball feet, the body with pierced scroll decoration, centred by enamelled plaques representing Roman emperors and their names SER GALBA VII and TITUS VESPASIAN XI and the coat-of-arms of the city of Hamburg, the hinged cover with an applied coat-of-arms, dated 1673, engraved with a scratch-weight Vog 109 Lod, and marked with maker's mark and town mark

description_en:
on three ball feet, the body with pierced scroll decoration, centred by enamelled plaques representing Roman emperors and their names SER GALBA VII and TITUS VESPASIAN XI and the coat-of-arms of the city of Hamburg, the hinged cover with an applied coat-of-arms, dated 1673, engraved with a scratch-weight Vog 109 Lod, and marked with maker's mark and town mark

21cm, 8¼in.
1878gr., 60¼oz
literature:
M. Rosenberg,
Der Goldschmiede Merkzeichen,
Frankfurt am Main, 1922, I, no. 2405(b).
W. Scheffler,
Goldschmiede Niedersachsen s, 1965, p. 446.
E. Schliemann et al,
Die Goldschmiede Hamburgs,
1985, II, no. 177 (2), illus. 248.
catalogue_note:
The Limoges enamel emperors are from the workshop of Jacques I Laudin (1627-1695). For a complete set of 12 such profiles from the Laudin workshop see: Sothebys, European Sculpture and Works of Art, London, 9 July 2008, lot 102. Servius Galba was the first of four emperors, who ruled in Rome during one year, 69 A.D, culminating in Titus Vespasian (Vespasian) the 10th emperor. The Titus Vespasian (Titus) depicted on this tankard is the 11th emperor and son of the 10th. There is a great contrast between Galba and Titus. The former was assassinated, the latter deified by the Roman senate.
The engraved arms on the cover under the applique are those of Ratlow of Holstein with probably those of Reinick of Nassau and Hesse.

literature:
P. M. de Winter, 'Recent Acquisitions of Italian Renaissance Decorative Arts, Part I: Incorporating Notes on the Sculptor Severo da Ravenna', in
The Bulletin of the Cleveland Museum of Art, vol. 73, no. 3, 1986, pp. 74-138, p. 114, fig. 102.
catalogue_note:
The precision and quality of finish of the present bronze, of which there are numerous known variations, justify the attribution of the casting to the workshop of Severo Calzetta da Ravenna. Along with Andrea Riccio, his name is associated with the valuable production of Renaissance bronze statuettes in northern Italy at the turn of the 15th and 16th centuries.
In 1986, Patrick M. de Winter published this example of the
Striding Satyr in a seminal article on the work of this sculptor, who was active in Padua, Ferrara and Ravenna (P. M. de Winter, op. cit., p. 114, fig. 102). The author draws an interesting parallel between the stance of the satyr and that of another in the background of an engraving by Mantegna,
Bacchanal with a Wine Vat, circa 1475 (The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, inv. 1986.1159). The composition can also be compared to Greco-Roman models such as the
Della Valle
Satyr in Rome (Musei Capitolini, inv. MC0004). Another example of the same model is in Brescia (Musei Civici, inv. no. BR136), another in La Spezia (Museo Civico, inv. no. B196), another in Rome (Museo di Palazzo Venezia, inv. no. 9243), and yet another, of comparable quality, was in the Yves Saint Laurent – Pierre Bergé collections (their sale, Christie's Paris, 25 February 2009, lot 484, described as attributed to Severo da Ravenna).
The modern history of this bronze, from the collection of Emma Budge (1852–1937), a German Jewish art lover and philanthropist, bears witness to the darkest hours of the 20th century in Europe. Originally from Hamburg, Emma married Henry (Heinrich) Budge (1840–1928), a German banker who emigrated to the United States and whose fortune was linked to the development of the railways. She left Germany for New York, where the couple settled in a house near Central Park. Returning to Hamburg in 1900, the Budges' villa became a cultural and social hub of the city, as well as a sanctuary for their extensive collection of European art. Emma and Henry were also renowned for their strong commitment to German charitable institutions, particularly in the fields of education and the arts.
When Emma died in 1937, although her will stipulated that the sale of her property should benefit Jewish charities, her collection was looted by the Nazi regime and auctioned in Berlin that same year, from 27 to 29 September. As the proceeds from this sale were never handed over to the rightful beneficiaries, the spoliation of the collection was officially recognised in 1947, and steps were taken to return it to the Budge heirs. An annotated copy of the catalogue of the 1937 forced sale, in National Art Library of the Victoria & Albert Museum, London, is an invaluable source of information on the fate of the looted works in the collection. The present bronze, lot 137 of the Budge sale, was then attributed, without any basis, to Francesco Bertos.
This lot is sold pursuant to a settlement agreement between the current owner and the heirs of Emma Budge.

catalogue_note:
The model of the present bronze, which was intended to hold a trident in his right hand and the reins of his chariot in his left, derives from the
Neptune in a Chariot Drawn by Two Sea Horses, formerly attributed to Jacopo Sansovino and now generally attributed to his pupil Tiziano Minio (1511/12-1552), circa 1540-1545.
Among the finest known examples are the one held at the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna (Neptune: inv. Pl. 5748; chariot: inv. 5911), another formerly in the Otto and subsequently Alfred Beit collections, London (see W. Bode, op. cit.; Christie’s, London, 7 December 2006, lot 162), and two further examples without the chariot, at the Victoria and Albert Museum (inv. A.80-1949) and the Palazzo Venezia, Rome (inv. 10782). Two other examples, at the Herzog Anton Ulrich-Museum, Brunswick (inv. Bro 108), and the Cleveland Museum of Art (inv. 1974.273), in which the chariot was cast in a single piece with a small base, are probably later casts taken from preexisting examples.
This model also inspired northern European sculptors during the third quarter of the 16th century. Pankraz Labenwolf (1492-1563) produced a variant in Nuremberg, retaining the same chariot but reversing the direction of Neptune’s movement (Walters Art Museum, Baltimore, inv. 54.2441).

literature:

C. Avery et al.,
Scultura III, cat. Tomasso Brothers Fine Art, London, 2010.
catalogue_note:
This fine, beautifully lacquered small bronze personification of Abundance is a brilliant example of the small statuettes that were being designed and cast during the heyday of bronze sculpture in Florence around 1600. Although they could serve as independent conversation pieces, such personifications were often part of ensembles of bronzes on pieces of furniture such as large cabinets inlaid with hardstones and other precious materials. Abbondanza’s pose is distinctly reminiscent of Michelangelo’s David while the overall conception of the female figure, with her interplay of strongly delineated folds and grooves, may be compared to Giambologna’s work, such as the large-scale Virtues for the Capella Grimaldi in San Francesco di Castelletto now in the Palazzo dell’ Università in Genoa which Giambologna made with the assistance of Pietro Francavilla around 1579-1587.
The facial type also compares to works from the ambit of Giambologna, such as two small bronzes of Venus after the bath and the Callipygian Venus attributed to one of the master’s successors in the princely collections of Liechtenstein and a further cast of Venus after the bath on the art market in 2010 which Avery attributed to Ferdinando Tacca.
1
Note especially the almost identical hairstyle of the Venus after the Bath and the emphasis on the eyelids. Such eyelids are also present in a small bronze of a Bagpiper in the Bode Museum in Berlin, which is attributed to Giambologna’s Florentine contemporary Valerio di Simone Cioli (1529-1599).
2
In this bronze the clothing is cut of similarly heavy cloth and the hands are equally enlarged. A lesser cast of the present figure was in the collection of Dr. Charles Avery, sold at Bonhams London, 11 December 2007, lot 494.

literature:
I. Favaretto, "Simona Bianco: Un Scultore del XVI secolo di fronte all'antico”, in
Numismatica e antichità classiche, Quaderni Ticinesi XIV, Lugano, 1985;
A. Luchs,
Tullio Lombardo and Ideal Portrait Sculpture in Renaissance Venice,
1490-1530, 1995;
F. de Mély, « L’Émeraude de Bajazet II et la Médaille du Christ d’Innocent VIII », in
Gazette des Beaux-Arts, juin 1898, pp. 487-493.
catalogue_note:
The stylistic characteristics of this right-facing profile of Christ, carved in mezzo rilievo, reflect the legacy of a sculptural tradition rooted in classical models that developed in the Veneto under the impetus of the Lombardo family and Simone Bianco. The finely delineated facial features, the flowing locks of the hair and beard, whose illusion of volume is enhanced by delicate drillwork, and the meticulous rendering of the folds and neckline of the tunic recall Venetian models from the first half of the 16th century, such as the
Profile of Christ attributed to Tullio Lombardo at the Kimbell Art Museum (inv. AP 2005.04), or the example by a follower of Simone Bianco that recently appeared at auction (Christie’s, Paris, 11 June 2025, lot 2). As in the latter example, the hollowed-out back of the present relief is a noteworthy feature of its execution.
This type of representation of Christ also appears in prints, as well as in medals and plaquettes dating from the third quarter of the 16th century. Notable examples include the plaquette depicting the
Profile of Christ at the Victoria and Albert Museum (inv. 59-1965), and a print from Enea Vico’s
Medaglie del Doni Fiorentino
(Ashmolean Museum, inv. WA1863.5693). This iconography of Christ the Redeemer draws on the
Vera Effigies Christi
(true image of Christ), an engraved emerald bearing Christ’s profile which, according to a tradition recorded in the late 15th century, was sent to Pope Innocent VIII around 1488, by the Ottoman sultan Bayezid II. Although the provenance and authenticity of this gemstone, now considered lost, remain uncertain, its influence in Renaissance Humanist circles is nonetheless evident.

literature:
F. Queyrel, R. Veymiers, « De « Scipion l’Africain » aux « prêtres isiaques » : à propos des portraits au crâne rasé avec cicatrice(s) », in
Individuals and Materials in the Greco-Roman Cults of Isis Agents, Images, and Practices, vol. 187, Leyden-Boston, 2018, pp. 384-412 & pp. 1046-1057;
A. Boström, « Ludovico Lombardo and the Taste for the all’Antica Bust in the Mid-Sixteenth-Century, Florence and Rome”, in
Large Bronze in the Renaissance, New Haven & London, 2003, pp. 155-179.
catalogue_note:
This powerful all'antica portrait of a beardless man with a shaved head and stern gaze is derived from Roman models from the Republican period or the early Empire. From the Renaissance to the 19th century, it was considered to be a portrait of Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus, known as Scipio Africanus (236 – 183 BC). In the early 20th century, it was hypothetically associated with representations of priests of Isis, but to this day, there is still no consensus on its identity. During the Renaissance, it was established that Pliny was the inventor of the myth that Scipio had introduced the ritual of daily shaving to Rome. In fact, he was referring to Scipio Aemilianus, the adopted grandson of Scipio Africanus. In any case, when this bronze was cast, the face was considered to be that of the consul and skilled Roman military strategist, whose name went down in history for his decisive action at the end of the Second Punic War, during the capture of Carthage.
In the 16th century, the heroic figure of Scipio, an exemplum of military and moral virtues, became extremely popular among Roman and Florentine aristocratic families. Ulisse Aldrovandi, in
Le Antichità della Città di Rome
(1556), was the first to recognise the hero of the Punic Wars in this model, of which he counted five ancient examples in Roman collections. In the 1562 edition, Aldrovandi describes in the Roman palace of Lorenzo Ridolfi, grandson of Lorenzo the Magnificent, a "Scipione Aphricano col busto vestido, & abbottonato su la spalla: ... E questa testa, clave & ha la veste ornata di oro; e sta sopra una base de la medesima felice " (A. Boström, op. cit., pp. 166-67). We thus learn that, at that time, a gilt bronze drapery was already associated with the ancient basalt head. At the end of the 16th century, we find it in the Roman palace of Federico Cesi; it was then engraved by Theodor Galle and published in 1598, then again in 1606, in llustrium imagines, ex antiquis marmoribus, nomismatibus, et gemmis expressæ, quæ exstant Romæ, maior pars apud Fvlvivm Vrsinvm
(plate 49). The bust then passed into the Ludovisi collection, before taking the name of its last owner and becoming the
Scipio Rospigliosi
(Palazzo Rospigliosi, Rome). Other ancient and later examples of this model are known, including one at the Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris (inv. BnF 15-57), two in Rome, at the Capitoline Museum (inv. MC 562) and the Chiaramonti Museum, and another on deposit at the Dallas Museum of Art (inv. 36.1997).
In the last third of the 16th century, the great Florentine families placed numerous orders for bronze busts after the Antique. Correspondence from Lorenzo Ridolfi mentions a series of antique busts cast in Rome for his collection; Antonia Boström now attributes them to Ludovico Lombardo (1507 – 1575), Tullio's nephew. The inventories of Rodolfi's Florentine palace in Via Tornabuoni, drawn up in 1564 and 1570, confirm the presence of such busts (cf. ibidem, p. 174, note 18). As early as October 1550, several letters addressed to Ridolfi by his secretary in Rome, Mariotto Giambonelli, reported on the progress of the casting of three busts of
Hadrian, Brutus and
Scipio
(cf. ibidem, pp. 160 and 170). Furthermore, still in Florence, we know that upon the death of Cosimo I de' Medici, in 1574, two bronze heads of
Scipio, contemporary with the Ridolfi busts, adorned the bedroom of the Grand Duke of Tuscany in the Palazzo Pitti. They were then described as portraits of
Scipio Aemilianus and
Scipio Africanus. It should be noted that, as in the present example, the eyes of the two heads from the Medici collections are not incised (Museo Nazionale del Bargello, inv. 137 and 125).
The ‘Pseudo-Scipio’ type from which this bronze derives, characterised by a shaved skull, a wrinkled forehead, marked brow ridges and a determined gaze, is an example of the ‘uncompromising’ style inspired by Roman portraits. It is not a slavish copy of an ancient head, but should rather be considered a pure product of the humanist imagination, nourished by the rediscovery of classical models. Some versions feature scars, which for some are the marks of wounds received in battle, and for others are the distinctive signs of the priests of Isis. In other versions, such as Galle's engraving, Pseudo-Scipio's shaved skull is intact. In fact, no scars are mentioned in Renaissance writings; they only became a distinctive feature of Scipio Africanus in the second half of the 18th century, as confirmed by Ennio Quirino Visconti when he wrote in 1817: "Winckelmann was the first to notice this characteristic mark that distinguished the portraits of Scipio. He uses this as an argument in favour of those who regard these portraits as belonging to Scipio the Elder, whom history tells us was wounded in the Battle of Tessin. " (cf. F. Queyrel, R. Veymiers, op. cit., pp. 388-89). Prior to 18 th century, only baldness characterised the supposed portraits of this illustrious figure in Roman history.
The present head of ‘Pseudo-Scipio’ therefore belongs to this second group, without a scar, and finds its best comparison in a bust from the Borghese collections, dating from the late 16th or early 17th century, with a bigio antico head and a giallo antico bust (Galleria Borghese, Rome, inv. LXXVI). Like the Borghese bust, our bronze differs from other versions of the same subject in that it has a less rounded face, refined cheeks and a more pronounced jaw, physical characteristics that are reminiscent of the typology of portraits of condottieri.

catalogue_note:
The model upon which the present bronze is based surmounted the Fiorenza Fountain in the gardens of the Villa di Castello. Commissioned by Cosimo de Medici, the fountain was designed by Niccolò Tribolo but left unfinished at the time of the artist’s death in 1550. The exact date of the bronze's later execution by Giambologna is contested in the scholarship – it may have been as early as 1560, or in the 1570s, when the sculptor was portrayed with the model by Hans van Aachen. It is generally accepted, however, that the
Fiorenza largely follows Tribolo’s original model, with Giambologna’s stylistic signature confined to the woman’s features. According to Vasari, the motif of a woman wringing water from her hair was chosen to present Florence as a flourishing city at the confluence of two rivers, the Arno and the Mugnone. It is clearly also an allusion to the
Venus Anadyomene type, famously conceived by Apelles and eagerly adopted by Italian Renaissance artists. Tribolo and Giambologna’s
Fiorenza thus follows in the footsteps Lorenzo de' Medici's
Birth of Venus ideology, which celebrated Florence as a rising, fertile and nourishing city.
The Fiorenza Fountain was transferred to the Villa Petraia in 1788, and it may have been at this time that the present cast was made.

catalogue_note:
The
Peasant Resting on a Staff, together with
The Bagpiper and
The Birdcatcher, exemplifies a more naturalistic strand of Giambologna’s œuvre. Although celebrated as the leading sculptor of Florentine Mannerism, Giambologna was also heir to an artistic culture rooted in Northern Europe.
A statuette of the present model is first documented at the Uffizi in 1601, when two silver statuettes were lent to Antonio Susini, including one described as “a small silver figure of a peasant wearing a hat and leaning on a little staff” (
Una figuretta d’argento di un villano con Capello con bastoncino che sappoggia su il bastone). The loan was presumably intended to facilitate the production of bronze casts after these models (see A. Radcliffe and Ch. Avery, op. cit., p. 165). In 1609, the inventory of Benedetto Gondi records
« un pastorino ... di mano e l’originale del Cavaliere Gian Bologna », which may correspond to the model presented here. Another example is documented in the collection of Charles I of England in 1612, having been inherited from his brother, Prince Henry, while a further example belonged to the collection of Rudolf II in Prague. These records attest to the model’s international circulation as early as the beginning of the 17th century.
These pastoral subjects, inspired by rural life, also evoke the Arcadian ideal of harmony between humankind and nature. Their origins can be traced to an earlier phase of Giambologna’s career, between 1577 and 1583, when he produced statues of peasants, both male and female, for the gardens of the Medici villa at Pratolino (now lost). These genre figures may be compared with another group created for the Medici, in the Boboli Gardens overlooking the Palazzo Pitti. The models of
The Peasant Resting on a Staff and
The Bagpiper may also allude to the shepherds Tityrus and Meliboeus, protagonists of Virgil’s first
Eclogue, a celebrated pastoral poem (see Max Wirgina in
Scultori Fiamminghi, op. cit., p. 177). Indeed, ancient sculpture offers numerous precedents for subjects drawn from pastoral life, and the present composition has previously been compared with a 2nd century marble sculpture in the Palazzo Colonna.
The exceptional quality of the present cast, evident in the delicacy of its modelling, the expressive treatment of the face, the elegant hands with their meticulously delineated fingernails, and the finely rendered curls escaping from beneath the hat, supports an attribution to Antonio Susini. The precision of the chasing further reinforces this attribution. An emblematic figure of Italian Mannerism, Susini was among the foremost sculptors and bronze-casters active in Florence around the turn of the 17th century. The extraordinary refinement of the bronzetti attributed to him reflects the meticulous standards of goldsmithing in which he had been trained. As Giambologna’s principal collaborator, Susini continued after the master’s death to produce bronze reductions based on the latter’s models.
Other casts of
The Peasant Resting on a Staff are held by the Staatliche Museen, Berlin (inv. no. 5030), the Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge (inv. M.2-1973), the Victoria & Albert Museum, London (inv. A.19-1971), and the Museo di Palazzo Venezia, Rome (inv. no. PV 10809). Further examples are found in important private collections of Renaissance bronzes, including the Claudia Quentin Collection. Finally, an example of
The Peasant Resting on a Staff, paired with
The Bagpiper, is currently featured in the exhibition
Scultori Fiamminghi, organised by M Leuven. They illustrate the rich artistic and cultural exchanges between Italy and the Low Countries during the Renaissance (see op. cit., pp. 176-179).

catalogue_note:
The theme of fight, offering the opportunity for endless variations on the nude body in motion, enjoyed immense popularity in 16th century Italian sculpture. Painters, printmakers and sculptors drew on the repertoire of Greco-Roman mythology, particularly the various combats of Hercules, as well as on biblical history, to find a pretext for depicting the tensed muscles of fighting figures.
As early as 1470-1490, Antonio del Pollaiuolo engraved a scene of the
Battle of Ten Nude Men, which would exert a considerable influence (Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, inv. 17.50.99). Indeed, the composition and style of the present group remain rooted in late 15th century prototypes. The elongated anatomy of the figures, their open mouths, seemingly releasing cries, and the frieze-like arrangement of the scene all evoke the painters and engravers of the
Quattrocento. The group should therefore be considered part of the tradition of small bronzes cast in northern Italy during the first decades of the 16th century, dominated by the seminal figure of Andrea Riccio. Stylistically, it differs from Florentine models of wrestlers, whose powerful musculature derives from Michelangelo, particularly those by Baccio Bandinelli, Vincenzo de’ Rossi and Giambologna.
The group of
Hercules and Antaeus held at the National Gallery of Art, Washington, formerly attributed to the goldsmith Francesco da Sant’Agata and now catalogued as “Padua, circa 1525”, provides the closest comparison (inv. 1942.9.119). A similar parallel may be drawn with the isolated figure of Antaeus, transformed into a
Running Man, an example of which is held at the Herzog Anton Ulrich-Museum, Brunswick, attributed to Francesco da Sant’Agata, circa 1520 (inv. Bro 29; see V. Krahn, 1995, op. cit., cat. 24, pp. 52-54).
Only five examples of the present model are known, comprising two distinct variants. In the Frankfurt group, the standing man threatens his opponent with a donkey’s jawbone (Liebieghaus, inv. 1279); this attribute identifies him as Samson fighting the Philistines. Two further examples of this variant featuring the jawbone are known: one offered by Sotheby’s in London, on 5 December 2012 (lot 36), and another, bearing the initials of the collector Boissel de Monville (1763-1832), sold by Christie’s in Paris, on 25 June 2019 (lot 132).
In another version, to which the present example and a further bronze in New York belong (Metropolitan Museum of Art, inv. 64.101.1562), the jawbone is replaced by a club, transforming the subject, according to different interpretations, into either
Hercules and Cacus or
Cain and Abel. However, the elongated anatomy of the figures seems at odds with the powerful physiques of Hercules and the monstrous giant Cacus, making the second interpretation, in our view, more plausible. The New York bronze, formerly in the collections of the Gotha Museum and subsequently Irwin Untermyer, was once attributed to Adriaen de Vries, circa 1590-1600. This unconvincing attribution has since been rejected, and the bronze is now catalogued as Netherlandish, 17th century.
Although the provenance and dating of the various known examples of this model have fluctuated over time, the most plausible assessment, in light of current knowledge, is that the present bronze was cast in northern Italy during the first third of the 16th century. Finally, it is worth noting that the Boissel de Monville example, described in 2019 as northern Italian, second half of the 16th century, has since been attributed to the Venetian sculptor Vittore Gambello, known as Camello, circa 1530 (Galerie Kugel, Maastricht, TEFAF 2020).

catalogue_note:
This statuette, of outstanding quality in both casting and chasing, is one of five known examples of the same model, which belongs to the
Venus pudica type. It derives from a Greek prototype attributed to Praxiteles and known as the
Aphrodite of Knidos. The goddess’s pose, modestly covering her nudity with her left hand, and her hair secured by a diadem, with two long locks falling over her shoulders, may also be compared with the antique marble
Venus Felix preserved in the Musei Capitolini, Rome (inv. 936), of which Antico cast a superb reduction around 1510 (Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna, inv. KK 5726). Praxiteles’ composition, known through numerous Roman bronze and marble statuettes, including the second-century AD
Venus with Dolphin in the British Museum (inv. 1898,0519.1), was among the key models for Italian Renaissance sculptors. The finest of the small bronzes of this type, all cast in northern Italy around the turn of the 16th century, and probably the prototype formerly belonging to the collection of Charles Drury Edward Fortnum, is now held at the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford (inv. WA1899.CDEF.B411; 26.1cm high). Jeremy Warren attributes this exceptionally precise casting to Francesco Raibolini (circa 1450-1517), known as “il Francia”, a painter, goldsmith and sculptor from Bologna.
In addition to the Ashmolean Museum example and the present statuette, three other bronzes of the same model are known. One, attributed to the circle of Severo da Ravenna, is held at the Musée du Louvre (inv. OA 9119; 27cm. high); another, formerly in the collection of John Pierpont Morgan, in gilt bronze and attributed to Severo, is now at the Frick Art Museum, Pittsburgh (inv. 1991.2; 26cm. high). The last one was recorded in the former Leon Bagrit collection, London, in the 1950s (whereabout unknown; see Y. Hackenbroch, op. cit., pp. 214–17). Another related small bronze, with variations, should also be mentioned: closer to the
Venus Felix type, but holding a cornucopia, it formerly belonged to the collection of Henry Pfungst (Sotheby’s, New York, 23–24 November 1984, lot 92; whereabouts unknown). Finally, another variant derived from the
Aphrodite of Knidos should be noted. This figure is unclothed, lacks both arms, and has her head slightly tilted to the right; a bronze example is held at the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna (inv. Pl. 5600; 23.1cm. high).
The attribution of the present model has given rise to considerable debate. Although a consensus seems to have emerged around Francia, or his circle, for the
Fortnum Venus, significant variations in casting quality, notable differences in facial features, and the uneven degree of surface finishing and cold-working among the known examples suggest that they originated from different foundries, all active in northern Italy, around Ravenna, Mantua and Padua, between the late 15th and early 16th centuries. To mention just one example, the Louvre bronze, which bears striking similarities to the present statuette, has at various times been attributed to an early 16th century Paduan workshop, associated with Andrea Riccio, compared with works by Antico and Bartolomeo Bellano, and, more recently, attributed to the workshop of Severo da Ravenna.
Severo da Ravenna was first documented in Ravenna in 1496; he was subsequently recorded in Padua from 1500 to 1509, before returning to Ravenna in 1511. The last recorded evidence of his activity is a payment received from Isabella d’Este in 1527 for a
Hercules. Several bronzes by Severo da Ravenna were formerly attributed to Riccio, notably by Leo Planiscig. The present model was among them, although, according to Jeremy Warren, its invention should be credited to Francia. In light of the current state of research on small Italian Renaissance bronzes, the present bronze can be attributed to Severo da Ravenna, like the example in the Louvre. Nevertheless, the quality of the casting and the precision of the chasing, particularly evident in the treatment of the hair, appear superior in the present example.
We are deeply grateful to Dr Jeremy Warren for taking the time to examine the present bronze and for his invaluable assistance with the research and preparation of this catalogue entry.

catalogue_note:
Flowers and fruit abound in the works of the Della Robbia family, a dynasty of sculptors and ceramists who mastered the technique of glazed terracotta in Florence during the Quattrocento and Cinquecento. These natural products feature not only in the spectacular frames that surround their tondos and reliefs, but also, occasionally, in independent compositions such as baskets of provisions or individual pieces of fruit
Since ancient times, Pliny the Elder has attributed numerous medicinal properties to the quince and praised its fragrance. Jeremy Warren ( op. cit., p. 413) also highlights the fruit’s association with Venus, who received a quince from Paris rather than an apple. By extension, the quince became a symbol of love and a gift with deep symbolic significance. Furthermore, Warren points out that the custom of newlyweds sharing a quince - already mentioned in Plutarch’s
Roman Questions at the end of the 1st century AD (
Quaestiones Romanae, 65) - was still practised during the Italian Renaissance.
Our quince (mela cognata) can be linked to a relatively small group of fruits attributed to the workshop of Giovanni della Robbia (1469-1529) made in the 1520s. Notable examples include an apple, a lemon and a quince held at the Casa Museo Rodolfo Siviero (Florence, inv. L. 41/1986), as well as a citron and an apple at the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford (inv. WA1888.CDEF.S19 and WA1888.CDEF.S20). Finally, note that a lemon was sold by Sotheby’s New York on 1 June 1991 (lot 162).

literature:
U. Mende,
Die Mittelalterlichen Bronzen im Germanischen Nationalmuseum, cat. Germanischen Nationalmuseum, Nuremberg, 2013, pp. 238-239, no. 77
catalogue_note:
Saint Adrian of Nicomedia was a Roman officer in the imperial guard at Nicomedia who converted to Christianity after witnessing the steadfastness of persecuted Christians during the reign of the emperor Maximian. According to his legend, Adrian publicly declared his new faith and was subsequently imprisoned and executed around 306 CE. Medieval and early modern artists usually represented him in armour because he had served as a soldier and military official, and because he became one of the principal military saints of northern Europe, especially in Flanders and the Low Countries. He is often shown with an anvil or hammer, referring to the manner of his martyrdom, since his limbs were said to have been shattered on an anvil. The lion that frequently accompanies him symbolized courage and martial virtue, but in the Flemish context it also alluded to the heraldic lion of Flanders and thus connected the saint directly with regional identity and devotion in places such as Geraardsbergen.
The cult of Saint Adrian became especially important in Geraardsbergen after his relics were translated there in 1175, transforming the town into a major pilgrimage centre in the medieval Low Countries. Pilgrims visited the abbey church to seek the saint’s protection against plague, sudden illness, and dangers associated with war and travel, and the town profited economically and politically from this growing devotion. By the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, Adrian’s cult had reached a high point: pilgrims’ badges bearing his image in armour with sword, anvil, and lion circulated widely across the region, demonstrating both the popularity of the shrine and the development of a thriving pilgrimage industry. In the early sixteenth century, at a time marked by recurring epidemics and political instability, devotion to Saint Adrian intensified further, and his image became closely tied to civic identity in Geraardsbergen, where annual processions, relic veneration, and the sale of devotional objects reinforced the town’s reputation as one of the foremost pilgrimage destinations in Flanders.

literature:

Meisterwerke Massenhaft. Die Bildhauerwerkstatt des Niklaus Weckmann und die Malerei in Ulm um 1500, exh. cat., Stuttgart, 1993;
C. Lichte and H. Meurer (eds.),
Die mittelalterlichen Skulpturen, 2. Stein- und Holzskulpturen 1400-1530: Ulm und südliches Schwaben, cat. Landesmuseum Württemberg, Stuttgart, 2007.
catalogue_note:
This elegant figure of an armoured saint bears a striking compositional and stylistic affinity with the
Saint George by Niklaus Weckmann now in the Liebieghaus, Frankfurt (inv. no. 73). Dated to between 1496 and 1499, Weckmann’s life-size figure was carved by the master from Ulm for the High Altar of the Abbey Church in Ochsenhausen, Upper Swabia.
The present figure’s gently undulating waves of hair, pointed lips with a serene smile, and forward moving stance compare closely to Weckmann’s prototype, indicating that the
Saint was probably carved by a sculptor in the master’s circle. Similar features are also seen in the male saints from the Talheim Altarpiece, which originated in Weckmann’s workshop around 1518 (Lichte and Meurer, op. cit., no. 77). Compare also the
Saint George from Weckmann’s retable in Salouf (Roller, op. cit., p. 360, fig. 516)
Niklaus Weckmann was one of the most prominent Late Gothic sculptors active in the Swabian city of Ulm, where he ran a prolific workshop from 1481. Much of his oeuvre was formerly attributed to Jörg Syrlin the Younger.

catalogue_note:
The year 1848 was a turning point both in French society and in Cordier’s career. It marked the definitive abolition of slavery in France, as well as the sculptor’s momentous encounter with Seïd Enkess (1821-?), a formerly enslaved man who had gained his freedom and become a professional model, and who came to Rude’s studio to offer his services. Cordier modelled his portrait in plaster and exhibited it at the Salon that same year.
This bust, whose history is closely intertwined with that of the
Vénus africaine, an example of which is also included in the present sale, marked the beginning of Cordier’s extensive ethnographic work. Alongside Queen Victoria (see previous lot for further details), the painter Rosa Bonheur (1822-1899) is known to have been among the first to acquire a bust of
Saïd
(whereabout unknown; see L. de Margerie and E. Papet, op. cit., p. 204, cat. 471).
The present example is a half-life-size reduction of the 1848 model. Other examples of comparable size and finish, generally paired with a bust of
La Vénus africaine, include those in the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, New York (see L. de Margerie and E. Papet, op. cit., cat. 500), and the Walters Art Gallery, Baltimore (inv. no. 542665).
Cordier later recalled in his memoirs: “My approach was timely, responding to a new subject: the revolt against slavery, and anthropology in its infancy” (see L. de Margerie and E. Papet, op. cit., p. 15).

literature: C. Chevillot, Oublier Rodin : La sculpture à Paris 1905-1914, ex. cat. Musée d'Orsay, Paris, 2009, cat. 56, p. 274; E. Lebon, Dictionaire des fondeurs de bronze d'art, Perth, 2003, p. 186.
catalogue_note:
Joseph Bernard began his studies in Lyon and received a scholarship in 1886 which enabled him to travel to Paris to attend the École des Beaux-Arts. Whilst reference is often made to Auguste Rodin's influence, Bernard never worked in his studio, preferring to work nights at a printing press to finance the early lean years of his career. His fierce independence is reflected in his oeuvre, as he experimented with unconventional techniques such as carving in taille directe and modelling directly in plaster rather than clay. Towards the end of his career, Bernard's own influence on French sculpture had become immense. As one critic of the 1927 Salon d'Automne wrote: 'if all sculptures influenced by Bernard were removed from the galleries, what would there be left?'

The first sketches for the Femme à la cruche, also known as Porteuse d'eau, date to 1905-1907. In 1908 the model was part of an important group of works by Bernard to be included in a contract with the foundry Hébrard. The life-size version now in the Musée d'Orsay was cast by Hébrard in 1912 and purchased by the French state in 1917 (inv. RF 3161). The model was exhibited at the Salon d'automne in 1912. The piece toured in the United States between 1913 and 1915 featuring in exhibitions in New York, Chicago, Boston and San Francisco.

RELATED LITERATURE
C. Chevillot, Oublier Rodin : La sculpture à Paris 1905-1914, ex. cat. Musée d'Orsay, Paris, 2009, cat. 56, p. 274; E. Lebon, Dictionaire des fondeurs de bronze d'art, Perth, 2003, p. 186.

catalogue_note:
The exaggerated musculature of the centaur Eurytion and the striking intensity of his expression suggest a collaboration between Albert-Ernest Carrier-Belleuse and Auguste Rodin. The work belongs to the Brussels period of the two sculptors’ careers, during which a terracotta version of
The Abduction of Hippodamia was first documented, in July 1871.
The contrast between the centaur’s brute animal strength and the graceful silhouette of his young captive places this composition within the tradition of abduction scenes, which flourished particularly in sculpture from the late sixteenth century onwards. The group recalls, in particular, Giambologna’s (1529–1608)
Rape of Deianira, one of the finest examples of which is held at the Staatliche Kunstsammlungen, Dresden (inv. H.23/95). Hippodamia’s arched body, as she vainly struggles to escape her captor’s grasp, echoes the dramatic tension of Giambologna’s group.
This expressive intensity finds a parallel in the treatment of the centaur. The taut muscles of his torso recall the twisting figures on the pedestal of
The Titans’ Gardener, a collaborative work executed circa 1875–1878 by Rodin after a drawing by Carrier-Belleuse (Musée des Beaux-Arts, Calais, inv. 973.7.1, for the drawing; Musée Rodin, Paris, inv. S.06739, for a glazed terracotta; see J. Hargrove, op. cit., 1977, pp. 256–258).
Eurytion’s contorted mouth, frozen in a cry of fury, also evokes the face of the allegorical figure in François Rude’s
The Departure of the Volunteers of 1792, created circa 1833–1836 for the Arc de Triomphe at the Place de l’Étoile in Paris. The violence of this silent scream anticipates that of the allegorical figure in Rodin’s
The Call to Arms, conceived in 1879, which likewise reveals the influence of Rude (bronze, Musée Rodin, Paris, inv. S.00469).

provenance: Studio sale of Baron Carlo Marochetti RA, Christie, Manson & Woods, London, 7 May 1868, lot 97; where acquired by Young, probably Sir John Young, later Lord Lisgar (1807-1879), Governor General of Canada from 1868 to 1872
catalogue_note:
This exceptionally rare bronze is a reduction of Marochetti's monumental statue of Washington which was made for the 1853 New York Crystal Palace Exhibition. Marochetti's colossal bronze was placed in the centre of the exhibitions great rotunda, but was subsequently lost in a fire. A related plaster maquette (measuring 63.5cm high) is in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London (inv. no. 1153-1868); it was given by the sculptor's widow to he museum in 1868. The present bronze is one of only two known versions of the model in bronze, the other is in the collection of the descendants of the sculptor at the chateau de Vaux-sur-Seine in France.
Born in Turin in 1805, Marochetti was educated in France at the École des Beaux-Arts, supplementing his studies with extended stays in Rome. After an unsuccessful attempt at winning the Prix de Rome, he subsequently chose to fund his own studies in the Eternal City. Drawn to the Romantic movement, Marochetti flourished under the patronage of Louis-Philippe's Orléans court, producing the
Assumption of Mary Magdalene for the Madeleine, a relief depicting the Battle of Jemappes for the Arc de Triomphe, and - his masterpiece - the equestrian monument to Emanuele Filiberto for the Piazza San Carlo, Turin. Following the 1848 revolution, he fled to Britain where he charmed Queen Victoria, becoming the unofficial court sculptor, creating a portrait of Prince Albert. His equestrian
Richard the Lionheart, shown at the Great Exhibition of 1851 and later cast for Old Palace Yard outside the Palace of Westminster, remains his best-known work. From his South Kensington studio and foundry, where Landseer's Trafalgar Square lions were cast, he ran a thriving practice until his death in 1867. The present bronze was sold in his studio sale at Christie's in 1868.

catalogue_note:
In the mid-19th century, when Cordier embarked on his extensive anthropological project, the representation of the Other - that is, any individual of non-European origin - remained an exceptional subject in sculpture.

Cordier modelled the plaster for the present work in 1851 and exhibited it for the first time at the Salon the following year, as a pendant to his Saïd Abdallah. Théophile Gautier admired the bust, which he called Vénus africaine, a name that conveyed the universal significance of her beauty by comparing it to that of the goddess. This association recalls the celebrated precedent of the Black Venus (now usually entitled Bather), sometimes attributed to Barthélemy Prieur, circa 1600, or alternatively to an Italian or Netherlandish sculptor. One example is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (inv. 26.14.15), and another at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt. Cordier’s models enjoyed considerable success, as evidenced by the two life-size bronze casts by Eck & Durand acquired by Queen Victoria for Prince Albert (Royal Collection, Osborne House, Isle of Wight, East Cowes, inv. no. RCIN 41510; H. 82 cm).

The present Vénus africaine is a half-life-size reduction of the 1851 model. Other examples of comparable size and patina, generally paired with a bust of Saïd Abdallah, include those in the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, New York (see L. de Margerie and E. Papet, op. cit., cat. 500), and the Walters Art Gallery, Baltimore (inv. no. 542665).

RELATED LITERATURE
L. de Margerie, E. Papet, Charles Cordier 1827-1905, l'autre et l'ailleurs, exh. cat. musée d'Orsay, Paris, 2004, pp. 204-209;
J. Marsden, European Sculpture in the Collection of His Majesty The King, vol. III, pp. 950-952, no. 680b;

literature:
"Roma scossa da una risata all scoperta dei falsi di Dossena", in
La Tribuna Illustrata, no. 5, Rome, 1 st
February 1959, pp. 20-21.
catalogue_note:
Alceo Dossena is one of the remarkable figures—as talented as they are enigmatic—who have left their mark on the history of sculpture. Originally from Cremona, he learnt the craft of stone and marble carving at a young age and became familiar with the models of medieval and Renaissance statuary. From the 1910s and 1920s onwards, he settled in Rome, where unscrupulous antique dealers, such as Alfredo Fasoli, commissioned works from him in the style of the ancients and Renaissance masters such as Donatello, Mino da Fiesole and the Pisani, which they then sold at exorbitant prices, passing them off as authentic, to an international clientele including the most prestigious American collections and museums.
Rumours began to circulate as early as 1926 about sculptures by a contemporary forger, but the scandal did not break until 1928. Whether innocent or a skilful manipulator, Dossena claimed that his works had only been sold as authentic without his knowledge. He was acquitted due to lack of evidence at the end of the trial, and severed all ties with the antique dealers who had employed him. He then invited H. W. Parsons, an art historian and consultant to numerous American museums, to his studio, and gave him access to all the documentation relating to his work.
The man who was yesterday’s alleged forger went on to build a solid reputation as an artist; from that point onwards and until the end of his career, Dossena signed and dated his works. Alongside the Quattrocento-style works he continued to produce, he developed a more personal style, which can be appreciated in this relief. It is comparable to another work at the Musei Civici di Pescia, entitled
Rosa Mundi and also dated 1936, which was exhibited in Rovereto during the recent exhibition dedicated to Dossena (see D. Del Bufalo, M. Horak (eds.),
Il falso nell’arte. Alceo Dossena e la scultura italiana del Rinascimento, exh. cat., Mart, Rovereto, 3 October 2021 – 9 January 2022, p. 213).
Twenty years after Dossena’s death, the myth surrounding this charismatic figure endured, and the Roman daily
La Tribuna Illustrata revisited the affair that shook the art world. In one of the photographs accompanying the article, Dossena is seen with two elegantly dressed women, evidently close acquaintances of the sculptor. The woman whom Dossena is looking at, on his right, is a Belgian baroness who at the time owned the present relief.

provenance: Private collection since 2007, in a Parisian Hôtel particulier
catalogue_note:
Luigi Bienaimé began his training at the Accademia di Belle Arti in Carrara, his hometown. Having been awarded a scholarship, he moved to Rome, where he joined Bertel Thorvaldsen’s studio on Via Quattro Fontane, immersing himself in the neoclassical aesthetic. A master of marble work, Bienaimé quickly became one of the Danish sculptor’s closest collaborators, and was entrusted with the management of his studio. From 1827 onwards, with his master’s encouragement, he also undertook major private commissions and gained an international reputation. He opened his own studio at 5 Piazza Barberini, which Tsar Nicholas I visited in person in 1845. The links between the sculptor and Russia can still be seen today at the Hermitage Museum, which houses at least five of his works. Bienaimé also carried out numerous commissions for German patrons, including the King of Württemberg, the Prince of Oldenburg and Count Dietrichstein.
The idealised features of our Bacchante’s face – carried away by the movement of the entrechats she is performing – and the dancing contours of her silhouette are in keeping with the legacy of her master’s models and, before him, those of Antonio Canova. Among Thorvaldsen’s works, this composition can be compared to the plaster cast of the Dancer, created around 1817 (Thorvaldsen Museum, Copenhagen, inv. A178). Further parallels can be drawn between the airy movement of the present Bacchante’s legs and Canova’s
Hebe, whose plaster cast dates from 1796 (Galleria d’Arte Moderna, Milan, inv. GAM 515), as well as between the suppleness of the folds in her dress and those of the
Dancer with her Finger on her Chin, whose plaster cast, dated 1809, is held in Possagno (Gypsotheca e Museo Antonio Canova, inv. 196).
Another example of the same model, dated 1846, was sold at Sotheby’s London on December 10, 2024, lot 177.

literature:

The Triumph of Motion. Francesco Bertos (1678-1741) and the Art of Sculpture. Catalogue Raisonné, Turin, 2008, p. 171, pl. 32, no. 27;
F. Mazzocca, M. De Vicenti,
Francesco Bertos e la Caduta degli angeli ribelli, exh. cat. Gallerie d’Italia, Vicenza, 2024, pp. 110-111, cat. 77 / III.6.
exhibited:
Vicenza, Gallerie d’Italia,
Francesco Bertos e la Caduta degli angeli ribelli, 11 October 2024 - 9 February 2025.
catalogue_note:
The three independent figures by Bertos offered in this sale testify to the sculptor’s creativity in his choice of subjects. Drawing on mythology and Ancient history, he devised distinctive interpretations of classical gods and heroes. His graceful figures often conceal an undercurrent of violence, as here, with the stone hidden behind the man’s back, evoking the young David poised to confront Goliath, and the threatening presence of a dagger. Comparable short swords can be found in the multi-figure group of
Cyllarus Wounded by the Lapiths
(Ch. Avery, op. cit., p. 178, pl. 9, no. 40). The headband tied around the head of the present
Gladiator also recalls the Greek taenia or Latin vitta, worn by victorious athletes.

Francesco Bertos

Italian, Venice, first half of the 18th century
Bacchus or Autumn

literature:
C. Avery,
The Triumph of Motion. Francesco Bertos (1678-1741) and the Art of Sculpture. Catalogue Raisonné, Turin, 2008, p. 171, pl. 34, no. 26;
F. Mazzocca, M. De Vicenti,
Francesco Bertos e la Caduta degli angeli ribelli, exh. cat. Gallerie d’Italia, Vicenza, 2024, pp. 104-105, cat. 58 / III.3.
exhibited:
Vicenza, Gallerie d’Italia,
Francesco Bertos e la Caduta degli angeli ribelli, 11 October 2024 - 9 February 2025.
catalogue_note:
Bertos’s distinctive artistic world is firmly rooted in 18th-century Venetian art, with dancing silhouettes and airy compositions. Charles Avery has indeed identified several parallels between Bertos’s work and the paintings of Giovanni Battista Tiepolo (1696 - 1770) and his son, Giovanni Domenico (1727 - 1804) ( op. cit., pp. 87–89). Of particular relevance is a drawing by Giovanni Domenico depicting the god of wine and drunkness, sold at Christie’s in Paris on 18 March 2004 (lot 68). His pronounced contrapposto and the gesture of the hand touching the top of his head are strikingly reminiscent of the composition of the present marble. This compelling comparison attests to the affinity between Bertos’s sculptural work and the sophisticated aesthetic of Venetian Rococo painting.
Stylistically, the present
Bacchus is consistent with Bertos’s œuvre, particularly in the deeply recessed eyes, slightly aquiline nose and strongly projecting brow ridges. A particularly pertinent comparison may be drawn with the group of
Bacchus and a Young Satyr, sold at Christie’s in London on 5 December 1994 (lot 82). The present work also demonstrates Bertos’s extraordinary technical virtuosity: the legs and arms are sculpted with admirable delicacy, rivaling the meticulous workmanship of the finest ivory carvers. The Inquisition, little inclined to fathom the mysteries of artistic genius, even accused Bertos of having made a pact with the Devil.

literature:

A Description and History of Powerscourt,
London, 1903, p. 47.
Bertel Thorvaldsen (1770-1844), scultore danese a Roma, exh. cat. Rome, Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna, 1989-1990, p. 41, fig.12;
S. Grandesso,
Bertel Thorvaldsen 1770-1844, Milan, 2015, p. 150.
catalogue_note:
Son of an Icelandic woodcarver, Thorvaldsen grew up in Copenhagen, where he was admitted to the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in 1781 to train as a sculptor. The young artist left for Rome in 1787, where he gravitated around the community of his fellow Danish emigrants. Among them were the antiquarian and scholar Jörgen Zoëga (1755-1809) and the painter and critic Asmus Jacob Carstens (1754-1798), both of whom had a considerable influence on Thorvaldsen's development as an artist, particularly with regard to his study of classical sculpture and the theories of the famous archaeologist Johan Joachim Winkelmann.
On the death of Antonio Canova in 1822, Thorvaldsen became the oldest and most respected sculptor in Rome, as confirmed by commissions such as the funerary monument to Pope Pius VII in St. Peter's Basilica (1823-1831), and appointments such as the presidency of the prestigious Accademia di San Luca (1828), a position previously held by Canova.
The original marble sculpture of
Mercury about to Kill Argus - completed by Thorvaldsen in Rome in 1822 (173 cm) - is housed in Copenhagen at the Thorvaldsen Museum (inv. A873). Six marble versions were produced during the artist’s lifetime, but also after his death, notably in the Lazzarini workshop in Carrara, which continued to produce works by the sculptor.
The Powerscourt Mercury
Our marble once belonged to the prestigious collection of the Viscounts of Powerscourt. In a book published in 1903, Mervyn Wingfield (1836-1904), the 7th Viscount, published an exhaustive description of the impressive collection assembled by his family, mainly during the second half of the 19th century, which included our marble.
This description, along with historical photographs, confirms the presence of our
Mercury in the sumptuous grand salon of Powerscourt, where it formed a pair with a marble of Mars and Venus after Canova. The provenance of our
Mercury is further confirmed at Powerscourt by a photograph dating from the last quarter of the 19th century, now in the collection of the Victoria & Albert Museum in London (inv. 3814:82/A-1953).
It was in 1665 that the politician Folliott Wingfield (1642-1717) was elevated to the peerage of Ireland as the 1st Viscount Powerscourt. Most of the collection at Powerscourt Estate (Enniskerry, County Wicklow) was gathered by Richard Wingfield (1815-1844), the 6th Viscount, and his son Mervyn. Both appear to have acquired their works at auction, as well as from Roman and Venetian art dealers.
Their descendants organized several auctions, including an first sale of books and manuscripts in 1927. An important part of the château’s contents, which certainly included our marble, was sold in 1948 by Allen & Townsend. In 1961, Powerscourt came into the ownership of the Slazenger family, before a massive fire ravaged the estate in 1974. A second sale, organised by Christie’s in 1984, sold the works that had survived the disaster.
We are grateful to Mr Alessio Costarelli for his kind assistance with the research and preparation of this catalogue entry.

bronze, golden-brown patina

catalogue_note:
The Laocoön is undoubtedly one of the most celebrated works of Ancient sculpture, an enduring icon whose discovery in Rome in 1506, near the remains of Nero’s
Domus Aurea, transformed the course of art history.
Shortly after its excavation, the group was acquired by Pope Julius II and installed in the Vatican Belvedere (Museo Pio-Clementino, inv. MV.1059.0.0). It depicts the terrible agony of the Trojan priest Laocoön and his sons as they are strangled by two sea serpents. In his
Natural History, Pliny the Elder described it as “the most admirable of all paintings and sculptures”. Renaissance observers held it in equally high esteem, among them Michelangelo, who regarded it as “a singular miracle of art”. Copies of the group were recorded as early as the years immediately following its discovery. A competition organised under Bramante and Raphael’s supervision was won by Sansovino, although his bronze has unfortunately been lost. In 1523, Baccio Bandinelli carved the first marble replica of the
Laocoön, intended as a diplomatic gift from Pope Leo X to Francis I which, against all expectations, never reached France (Palazzo Pitti, Florence, inv. 284).
In 1543, Primaticcio (1504-1570) produced a life-size bronze replica for the Château de Fontainebleau (inv. no. MR 3290). Two further life-size replicas were cast in 1687 by Jean-Balthasar Keller; one is now at the Palais-Bourbon in Paris, and the other at Houghton Hall in Norfolk. Another life-size example, cast in 1817 by Auguste-Jean-Marie Carbonneaux, appeared in successive sales of three of the most emblematic British collections of the 19th century - Fonthill Abbey, Stowe and Hamilton Palace - and was recently sold by Sotheby’s in London (1 July 2026, sold for £13.6 million).
The celebrated Vatican marble also inspired countless reductions, predominantly in bronze, in an extraordinary variety of sizes and finishes. The present example is distinguished by its rare, impressive scale and the outstanding quality of its sand casting, this technique suggesting a French origin of the bronze. The precision of the casting is particularly evident in the details of the hands, feet and faces, as well as in the sharply defined folds of the drapery. The skillful chasing, visible in several areas where inevitable casting flaws have been corrected, the excellent surface finish - particularly the matte punchwork in the hair and beard - and the bronze’s warm patina all point to an execution in the first decades of the 19th century. Its execution must therefore be dated to the period during which the celebrated Vatican marble remained in Paris, having arrived at the Museum central des arts (renamed Musée Napoléon in 1803) in July 1798, or shortly after its departure in October 1815, following the fall of the Empire.

bronze, dark brown patina; on a verde antico marble socle

provenance:
Private collection, Paris, since the 1960s;
Thence by descent to the present owners.
catalogue_note:
The present
Écorché Horse is a reduction of the
Cavallo Mattei, a half-life-size bronze (90.5cm. high) now held at the Palazzo Vecchio in Florence, whose pose derives from the
Marcus Aurelius on the Capitoline Hill in Rome. Probably executed around 1598, as evidenced by an engraving by Carlo Ruini
(fig. 1), it has been regarded by some scholars as a study by Giambologna for his equestrian statue of
Cosimo I de’ Medici
(circa 1594; Piazza della Signoria, Florence).
In 1703, the
Cavallo is documented in Rome, at the villa of Duke Giuseppe Mattei, from whom it takes its name. It subsequently entered the collection of Cardinal Fesch, Napoleon I’s uncle, and was included in his sale in Paris on 17 June 1816 (lot 263). It reappeared in London in 1913, where it was acquired by the American art historian Charles Loeser (1864–1928), who, upon his death, bequeathed it, together with part of his collection, to the city of Florence. Three further casts of the same size were produced by Luigi Valadier and his son Giuseppe between the late 18th and early 19th centuries. One, from the Torrie collection and formerly owned by Sir James Erskine, is now at the University of Edinburgh; another is held at the Museum of Fine Arts in Springfield, Massachusetts; and the third, formerly in the collections of the Dukes of Northumberland and subsequently owned by Baron Alexis de Redé (1922–2000) at the Hôtel Lambert, was sold by Sotheby’s in Monaco on 26 May 1975 (lot 187), and later by Christie’s in London on 4 July 2013 (lot 10).
In 1794, Francesco Righetti, the celebrated Roman sculptor, goldsmith and bronze founder, who had trained under Luigi Valadier, published a sales catalogue of the bronze reductions produced in his workshop after some of the most renowned models of Antiquity and the Modern Era. Among the bronzes offered was “ a flayed horse by Mattei, 20 Roman sequins
”, a model that Righetti had undoubtedly had the opportunity to study during his time in Valadier’s workshop.
Renowned for the quality of their casting and the perfection of their chasing, Righetti’s bronzes were particularly sought after by an international collector visiting Rome, an essential stop on the Grand Tour, from the 1780s onwards. Buoyed by his success, he opened a second workshop in Naples in the early 19th century. The precision of the present
Écorché Horse, which renders in the finest detail an equine musculature observed with exceptional accuracy, and its rich brown patina, which accentuates the forms, are consistent with Righetti’s autograph bronzes and support its attribution to this master bronze founder.
We are deeply grateful to Dr Jeremy Warren for taking the time to examine the present bronze and for his invaluable assistance with the research and preparation of this catalogue entry.

literature:

Le Livre des Collectionneurs,
Paris, 1885, p. 662 (“
Two birds pecking at one another carry the King’s and Queen’s medallions to the top of an altar upon which rest two flaming hearts. One must see the work for oneself to appreciate the extent to which it is imbued with realism and delicacy. The birds are depicted as lifelike as in nature.”);
S. Lami,
Dictionnaire des sculpteurs de l'école française au dix-huitième siècle, vol. II, Paris, 1911, p. 225.
C. Streeter, 'Two Carved Reliefs by Aubert Parent', in
The J. Paul Getty Museum Journal, vol. 13, 1985;
A.-M. Kerneis,
Aubert Parent: 1753-1835, Mémoire de maîtrise, Lille III, 1989.
catalogue_note:
Aubert Parent, a native of Cambrai, was an expert wood carver, sculptor, draftsman and architect who was trained under Etienne Pierre Adrien Gois (1731-1823) at the Académie Royale in Paris. Parent’s career was launched by the presentation of an elaborate masterpiece panel, entitled
Allégorie de l’amour de Louis XVI pour ses sujets, to Louis XVI at Valenciennes, the artist’s native town, in 1777 (château de Versailles, inv. MV8614). Centred upon an elaborate vase filled with flowers, it is emblazoned with a large portrait medallion of Louis XVI, which is, in turn, flanked by cornucopiae and trophies. The King was so enamoured by Parent’s gift that he had it placed in his salle à manger intérieure at Versailles (the royal dining room) so that he might admire it every day.
The success of the Louis XVI led Parent to establish himself as the trompe-l’oeil wood carver par excellence for aristocratic patrons in France and abroad, including Catherine the Great of Russia. Collin Streeter concludes, ‘
Launched by such public royal approval, Parent could hardly fail to succeed. The private commissions that he exhibited at the Salon de la Correspondence from 1779 to 1783 reveal a pattern of patrons belonging to court rather than Parisian circles’
( op. cit., p. 61). Although it does not appear in the Salon catalogues, our relief is likely part of this production; undoubtedly commissioned by a patron wishing to pay homage to the King and Queen.
Following the fall of the French monarchy, Parent fled France, first to Switzerland and then to Prussia, where he produced a pair of high-relief flower bouquets dedicated to Frederick William II of Prussia which is today in Berlin’s Kunstgewerbemuseum (inv. nos. K3041 and K3042). Parent went on to become a member of the Berlin Academy of Fine Arts and exhibited at the Marstallgebäude on Unter den Linden between 1797 and 1812.

catalogue_note:
In his
Metamorphoses, Ovid relates the myth of Hermaphroditos, son of the goddess Aphrodite and the god Hermes, whom the poet describes as having inherited his parents' great beauty. One day, while he is bathing in a pool, the nymph Samalcis falls in love with him, forcibly embraces him and begs the gods to join their bodies in perpetuity. This enforced fusion turns Hermaphroditos into a being who is both male and female.
The most famous portrayal of this mythological figure is the antique marble of the
Sleeping Hermaphrodite, made in the second century BCE (now in the Musée du Louvre, inv. no. MR 220; fig. 1). The combination of the figure's sleeping posture and the drapery creates a mise-en-scène that reveals the duality of the figure's sexual attributes in two stages. Discovered in Rome in the 1620s near the Baths of Diocletian, the marble was restored by Bernini (1598-1680), who added the mattress on which the figure rests. In 1638, the
Sleeping Hermaphrodite entered the collection of Cardinal Scipione Borghese (1577-1633), who displayed it in his famous Roman villa (where it remained until 1807).
The sculpture continued to be a source of fascination for many decades after its discovery and the model was disseminated throughout Europe by means of numerous copies in different sizes and materials. Some rare examples are mentioned in private collections of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, notably that of Louis XIV (Bronze de la Couronne no. 30, MV 7778).

catalogue_note:
This large and finely carved oval marble bas-relief depicts two Roman soldiers engaged in one to one combat on horseback. Each cavalryman holds a spear in his right hand and a shield in his left and the horses rear up on their hind legs as they meet in battle. The encounter is set in a wooded landscape with a distant view of a classical temple on a hill with a row of large tents on the plain below, skilfully carved in low relief. It is a scene of great drama, with the sense of a strong wind blowing from left to right animating the horses' manes and the billowing cloak of the right hand soldier.
The generic iconography of the soldiers’ uniforms and landscape prevent a definitive identification of the classical subject matter. It has been suggested that the scene might represent the combat between Titus Manlius and Geminus Mencius, but other battles from Roman history could also fit this subject.
Equally, this intriguing relief defies attribution as to the sculptor. The story is told in a ‘pictorial’ manner, that is to say there is a lot of expertly carved incidental detail, such as the trees, carved in high relief, the foreground with a broken tree stump and clouds in the distance suggesting a stormy day, befitting the dramatic events. The interest in an ancient historical theme might indicate a sculptor from the neoclassical period after the 1780s, but this is inconsistent with the overall ‘pictorial’ treatment described. This suggests that the marble was carved in the period from around 1750 to 1780, a period when the late Baroque style was transitioning into the Neoclassical. In Florence this includes sculptors such as Innocenzo Spinazzi, Giovanni Antonio Cybei and Francesco Carradori whilst in Rome there are sculptors such as Filippo della Valle, Bartolomeo Cavaceppi and Carlo Albacini. But one cannot rule out a sculptor either from Naples or from the North of Italy. The high quality of carving and substantial dimensions of this marble suggest that there is every possibility that further research could result in solving the attributional puzzle of this highly decorative sculpture.

catalogue_note:
Similar to François Duquesnoy’s Children, allegorical groups in the form of putti personifying the Senses, the Elements or, as in this case, the Seasons, underwent significant development in Baroque sculpture in the Low Countries, particularly in Brussels, Antwerp and Amsterdam.
From the third quarter of the 17th century onwards, in his design for Amsterdam Town Hall – in which childhood features prominently – Artus Quellinus the Elder established the foundations for this genre of allegorical iconography, which Rombout Verhulst, like Grupello, would help to disseminate in Brussels, Düsseldorf and elsewhere in the Netherlands. In the first third of the 18th century, the Antwerp workshop of Jan Pieter van Baurscheit the Elder, in turn, produced numerous groups of children ( kindertje), personifying in particular the cycle of the Seasons or other allegorical themes, intended for gardens and architectural decorations.
