title: French, 18th century, after François Girardon (1628 - 1715)
medium: bronze, brown patina
description:
French, 18th century, after François Girardon (1628 - 1715)
The Rape of Proserpina by Pluto

bronze, brown patina
56.5cm., 22¼in.
description_en:
French, 18th century, after François Girardon (1628 - 1715)
The Rape of Proserpina by Pluto

bronze, brown patina
56.5cm., 22¼in.
provenance:
With Maurice Segoura, Paris, 1970s;
From whom acquired, private collection, London.
literature:
G. Bresc-Bautier, G. Scherf (eds.),
Bronzes français de la Renaissance au Siècle des Lumières, exh. cat. musée du Louvre, Paris, October 2008 - January 2009, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, February - May 2009, J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles, June - September 2009, pp. 258-265;
R. Wentley,
French Bronzes in the Wallace Collection, London, 2002, pp. 54-56.
catalogue_note:
Recounted in Ovid’s
Metamorphoses
(V, 351), the scene is set in the Sicilian countryside. Proserpina, daughter of Ceres and Jupiter, is gathering flowers when Pluto, god of the Underworld and son of Saturn, abducts her, despite the resistance offered by the young nymph Cyane, who attempts to thwart the abductor.
Around 1674–75, François Girardon, First Sculptor to the King and, alongside Charles Le Brun, one of the principal masterminds behind the artistic commissions of the Sun King, received the commission for a large marble group depicting the
Abduction of Proserpina. It was intended to represent Fire in a series devoted to the elements, forming part of an ambitious scheme conceived by Le Brun for the Parterre d’Eau at Versailles. In addition to Girardon’s marble, this unrealised project called for the creation of two further groups on the same theme: the
Abduction of Orithyia by Boreas and the
Abduction of Cybele by Saturn, the former entrusted to Gaspard Marsy and Anselme Flamen, the latter to Thomas Regnaudin. Completed in 1689, Girardon’s group was not dated until its delivery in 1699, when it was installed at the centre of the Colonnade (château de Versailles, inv. MR 1865).
The earliest documented reductions after Girardon’s marble stand approximately one metre high, such as the bronze at Versailles, which was paired with an
Abduction of Orithyia, delivered in 1693 and installed in the Oval Salon in the King’s Apartments (château de Versailles, inv. MV 7953). Eighteenth-century auction catalogues attest to the popularity of these bronze reductions, which were often presented in pairs with an
Abduction of a Sabine after Giambologna’s model or, as in the aforementioned example, with an
Abduction of Orithyia after the marble by Marsy and Flamen.
Further reductions were subsequently produced in dimensions similar to those of the present example, measuring between 55 and 60 cm in height. A comparable example, acquired in Paris in 1715 for Augustus the Strong, is preserved in Dresden (circa 1700, H. 57 cm; inv. H4 153 / 008). Another is in the Wallace Collection (circa 1700-25, H. 54.6 cm; inv. S170), a third at Versailles (circa 1699, H. 55 cm; inv. MV 8629.1), and a fourth in the musée du Louvre (18th century, H. 57 cm; inv. OA 12241).
It is worth noting that the present bronze’s naturalistic, tiered terrasse is usually found on the larger versions, whereas examples of comparable dimensions often feature a square base, finished to varying degrees. The previously mentioned examples at Versailles and Dresden are, however, notable exceptions, as both display a naturalistic terrasse comparable to that of the present bronze.

Venus Victrix acquired from Sotheby’s London, 9 December 2005, lot 86; both in the same private collection, Belgium; thence by descent to the present owner, Belgian noble collection.
catalogue_note:
The model for the present
Venus, victorious in the Judgement of Paris, is a free interpretation after the Antique. The movement of the body and of the left hand, modestly concealing her nudity, derive from the
Medici Venus, while the outstretched left arm, showing the apple of discord, recalls the pose of the
Flora Capitolina.
The figure of
Cleopatra, mortally bitten by an asp, closely follows the composition of the marble formerly belonging to the French royal collections, documented in the park of the Château de Versailles in 1697 and at Marly the following year. Transferred to the Louvre Museum at a later date, this marble is now attributed to an Italian, probably Tuscan, sculptor and dated to the last quarter of the 16th century (inv. MR SUP 2). The model was sufficiently renowned in the 17th century for Hubert Lesueur to cast it in bronze for Charles I of England.
Although they come from different provenances, these two statuettes display striking stylistic similarities, particularly in their classicising proportions, facial features with unincised eyes, treatment of the hair and drapery, and identical small, integral octagonal terraces. These correspondences indicate that they almost certainly originated from the same artistic centre in the second half of the 17th century.

Thence by descent to the present owner, Belgian noble collection.
catalogue_note:
Arriving in Munich in 1726, where he worked for the court of the Elector of Bavaria, Maximilian III Joseph, Simon Troger occupies a singular place in 18th century European sculpture. His art is distinguished by the combination of ivory and wood, a technique much in vogue at the time, which the sculptor brought to an exceptional degree of refinement. His ambitious, sometimes monumental compositions earned him international renown. Among the works most representative of his distinctive Baroque style, characterised by a taste for the unusual and by contrasts between materials, his spectacular
Sacrifice of Isaac proved so successful that seven versions were produced. One is held at Palazzo Madama in Turin (185cm. high; inv. 65/AV), while another, even larger, is in the Museo di Santa Giulia, Brescia (263cm. high).
Troger also excelled in the production of statuettes intended for collectors’ cabinets, employing the same combination of materials: ivory for the flesh, glass for the eyes, and wood for the clothing and accessories. Drawing on a repertoire of established poses, which he adapted by varying the accessories and the positions of the arms and legs, the sculptor created astonishing figures of beggars and vagabonds, whose destitution contrasts with the preciousness of the materials employed. His
Kombinationfiguren dispense with any reference to biblical or mythological narratives, instead translating into three dimensions fleeting glimpses of human misery, such as those depicted in the previous century by Jacques Callot, and later by the French
Peintres de la Réalité, and the Dutch masters. Troger’s works are held in numerous public collections, notably the Deutsches Historisches Museum in Berlin, the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam, and the Bayerisches Nationalmuseum in Munich.
The present pair of beggars, remarkable for their particularly imposing dimensions, is fully representative of this body of work. The expressiveness of the faces, the attention to realistic detail, and the contrast pushed to the point of unease-as exemplified here by the elderly woman exposing a withered breast to an infant-are characteristic of Troger’s art. Like vanitas figures, these decaying bodies, with their deeply lined faces and toothless smiles, confront the viewer with a meditation on the fragility of the human condition.
A group depicting a seated beggar woman with her child, from the same composition, is preserved in Dresden, in the Green Vault (Grünes Gewölbe, SKD, inv. II 212).

description_en:
Attributed to Pieter Quast (1605-1647)
Northern Netherlandish, The Hague or Amsterdam, circa 1635-1645
Relief with the Five Senses

polychromed terracotta
23 by 30cm., 9 by 11¾in.
literature:
M. Leeflang, ‘Een uniek terracotta reliëf’,
Catharijnebrief. Magazine van Museum Catharijneconvent 98, no. 3, 2008, pp. 8-9;
J. Leeuwenberg, ‘Beeldhouwwerk van de schilder Pieter Quast’,
Bulletin van het Rijksmuseum 14, 1966, pp. 60-64.
catalogue_note:
Pieter Jansz. Quast was born in 1609 in Amsterdam, but spent a substantial part of his short career in The Hague, where he was a member of the Guild of Saint Luke and married a local woman in 1638. There, he was the tutor of the young Prince William II, the son of Frederik Hendrik, whose surviving drawings bear a strong resemblance to Quast's work. Quast specialized in painting, engraving, and drawing figures from everyday life. He placed farmers, beggars, quacks, and drunkards in compromising situations to humorously illustrate what was considered moral and immoral at the time. A Hague notary's report suggests that Quast himself was not of impeccable character either: he once held a knife to the throat of a church notable who accused Quast's wife, whether falsely or not, and threatened to kill him. Apart from his unusual behavior, Quast was also one of the few painters of the Golden Age to venture into sculpture. The Rijksmuseum owns a gilded terracotta relief of two fighting men, held apart by spectators, which strongly resembles the above scene from Quast's own life. It is signed:
P. Quast and dated 1628 on a violin lying in the foreground.
In an article in the Rijksmuseum Bulletin from 1966, Jaap Leeuwenberg attributed two further reliefs representing the
Five Senses to Quast on the basis of the signed
Fight between two men: one terracotta relief with badly damaged edges in Museum the Lakenhal in Leiden and a relief in wood in what is now the Israel Museum in Jerusalem.
1
A terracotta relief representing the
Flagellation in Museum Catharijneconvent in Utrecht was attributed to Quast more recently by Micha Leeflang.
2
The resemblances between the general conception of the reliefs, such as the size and the lower edge with a ledge designed to accommodate a frame, and the style of the figures -note especially the style of the flowing drapery, the hats and the near-identical small dog in the
Fight and the Jerusalem
Five Senses
- suggest Leeuwenberg and Leeflang had a strong case. The present relief is a further version of the Jerusalem relief which Leeuwenberg attributed to Quast and cements this composition's connection to him further because it is skilfully polychromed, as one might expect from a painter. Furthermore, it proves that the Jerusalem
Five Senses was also made in terracotta, which seems to have been the material Pieter Quast preferred for sculpture.
1
Leeuwenberg, op. cit.
Museum de Lakenhal: inv. no. B 27; Another version of the Lakenhal relief is in the Science Museum in London, catalogued as German, 18th century, inv. No. A27810.
2
Leeflang, op. cit.

description_en:
South Netherlandish, late 16th/ early 17th century
After Frans Floris de Vriendt (1590-1570)
Relief with Hercules and the Pygmies

marble
62 by 41.5 by 8cm., 24⅜ by 16⅜ by 3⅛in.
provenance:
Noble collection, Germany, until 1995;
Hugo Ruef Munich, 29-30 June 1995, lot 1610 (one of a pair); with Siegfried Kühnke Kunsthandel, Pähl-Fischen, Germany, 1995; private collection, Berlin, 1995 until 2015; with Kunsthandel Dr. Rainer und Brigitte Jungbauer, Straubing, Germany, 2015; private collection, Flemish-Brabant, Belgium
literature:
B. Falk, ‘Hybris und Strafe. Zwei niederländische Marmorreliefs des 17. Jahrhunderts‘,
Weltkunst. Aktuelle Zeitschrift für Kunst und Antiquitäten 66, no. 4, 15 February 1996, pp. 332-334
catalogue_note:
This spectacular marble relief, populated by no fewer than sixty male nudes, relates the entire legend of Hercules and the Pygmies as told by Philostratus (c. 190–230 CE) in the
Eikones, a description of a Neapolitan gallery of paintings.
1
Starting at the top left the Gods of Olympus look on as Hercules crushes the giant Antaeus, son of Poseidon and Gaia, in the air. In the lower left corner we see Antaeus’ body lamented over at the proper right hand by his brothers, the Pygmies. On the right Hercules is lulled to sleep by Hypnos as the Pygmies emerge from the earth and attempt to take their revenge, assaulting his limbs, stealing the hero’s club, and setting fire to his hair. Centrally in the background we see Hercules moving away after waking up. Under his left arm he carries his lion’s skin from which the legs of the Pygmies protrude for Hercules woke and laughed as he gathered up the army of little men effortlessly.
The relief is derived from a lost painting by Frans Floris (1590–1570) which was engraved and disseminated by Cornelis Cort (1533–1578).
2
When the relief appeared at auction in Munich in 1995 it was together with a pendant, a relief of
Apollo flaying Marsyas after a print by Melchior Meier (active 1572–1582) which reappeared in the Important Old Master Paintings sale at Sotheby’s New York on 26 January 2012 (lot 353).
3
Given the authorship of the model it is tempting to attribute to the relief to Frans Floris’ son Cornelis, who was responsible for various major sculptural ensembles in the Southern Netherlands. His interest in texture and the execution of certain details such as the architecture in the background and the ringlets that make up the hair of the figures certainly compare to his work. However, Cornelis was at the heart of the Floris-style, which Netherlandish sculptors took to patrons across Europe. Such complex reliefs inspired by graphic sources were especially a staple of Netherlandish sculptors working in Germany and Eastern Europe in the second half of the sixteenth century. The carvings were often part of the decorations of the studioli of noblemen, reception rooms in which art collections were displayed. Philip the Magnanimous, Landgrave of Kassel (1504–1567), for example, commissioned two Netherlandish sculptors to supply a series of
Labours of Hercules for his
Alabasterzimmer.
4
South Netherlandish artists also furnished tombs with series of reliefs. A case in point is the set of historical battle scenes Alexander Colin (1527–1612) provided for the tomb of Maximilian I in the Hofkirche Innsbruck.
5
Due north, in Wroclaw and Lviv, Netherlandish sculptors such as Gerhard Hendrik and Hendrik Horst carved similarly populous reliefs for epitaphs and altars using prints by Maarten van Heemskerck and Maerten de Vos around 1600.
6
That the subject
Hercules and the Pygmies had some currency in palatial settings in particular is proven by several known painted versions of the legend. Dosso Dossi’s (1490–1542) rendition which is now in Graz was meant for Ercole II d’ Este’s (1508–1559) ducal palace in Mantua. A pair of pictures showing Hercules asleep and awake painted by Lucas Cranach the Younger (1515–1586) in 1551 was on display in the
Riesensaal
(Giant’s room) in the castle of the Duke Moritz of Saxony in Dresden.
7
There Hercules’ might and vigilance would reflect upon the noblemen who commissioned the objects. It is safe to say that the present relief, especially in combination with the relief of Apollo flaying Marsyas, was also meant to remind the onlooker of the might and preparedness to exact justice of the object’s noble owner.

Elder Philostratus, Younger Philostratus, Callistratus, London, 1931, Book II, 22;
2

5
C. Haidacher and D. Diemer,
Maximilian I. Der Kenotaph in der Hofkirche zu Innsbruck, Innsbruck, 2004;
6
P. Oszczanowski, ‘Wroclawskie epitafium Uthmannów – rcesz o “niderlandyzmie wyuczonym”’, M. Kapustki et al.
(eds.),
Niderlandyzm na Slasku i w krajach osciennych, Wroclaw, 2003, pp. 203-216; A. Lipinska, ‘Eastern outpost. The sculptors Herman van Hutte and Hendrik Horst in Lviv c. 1560-1610’, F. Scholten et al. (eds.),

I. Wardropper (ed.),
From the Sculptor’s Hands. Italian Baroque Terracottas from the State Hermitage Museum, exh. cat. The Art Institute of Chicago, Chicago, 1998, pp. 46-49.
catalogue_note:
This highly expressive torso of the central figure in the
Laocoön group is a study by a sculptor seeking to draw the finest lessons from the sources of classical sculpture.
For having profaned the temple of Neptune, the priest Laocoön and his two sons were condemned to die, strangled by two sea serpents. This pivotal episode in the Trojan War offered sculptors one of the most poignant representations of suffering, both physical - the struggle of a body seeking to escape a deadly embrace - and psychological, as of a father condemned to witness the deaths of his children.
Rediscovered in Rome in 1506 among the ruins of Nero’s
Domus Aurea, the marble was acquired by Pope Julius II, who installed it in a specially designed courtyard at the Vatican (Museo Pio-Clementino, inv. MV.1059.0.0). It subsequently became one of the most admired antiquities in Rome. From the 16th century onwards, numerous sculptors attempted the challenging task of modelling the
Laocoön. Notable examples include two terracotta versions held at the Princeton University Art Museum, one dating from the late 16th or early 17th century, and the other from the 17th century (inv. Y1968-118 and Y1968-119). Another noteworthy example is the terracotta by Stefano Maderno, circa 1630, formerly in the collection of the Venetian abbot Filippo Farsetti (Hermitage Museum, Saint Petersburg, inv. 553).
In the present example, the sculptor focuses his study on the central figure of the priest Laocoön. The clean breaks below the shoulders, at the knees and at the upper thigh suggest that the clay may have been dried and fired in separate sections to prevent it from cracking. If this hypothesis is correct, the limbs, assembled after firing, may subsequently have become detached. Alternatively, the work may have been conceived in its present form. The elongated proportions of the torso and thigh, together with the facial features, allow comparison with models produced in Rome or northern Italy during the first half of the 17th century.

The scene depicts the miracle of the palm tree, an apocryphal episode from the childhood of Christ from the Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew, probably written between the 7th and 8th centuries. As the Holy Family flees Bethlehem for Egypt, the Child commands the palm tree beneath which the Virgin is resting: ‘Bend down, tree, and feed my mother with your fruit!’ (chapter 20). catalogue_note:
This large ivory plaque carved in deep, almost three-dimensional relief, emulates Bartholomeus Spranger’s popular painting of the Roman playwright Terence’s adage
Sine Cerere et Baccho friget Venus. Painted for Emperor Rudolf II in Prague around 1590 and propelled into popular culture by a print by Jan Harmensz. Muller, Spranger’s painting pioneered the representation of the proverb, which translates as
Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus freezes, as a celebration of the delights of food and wine by emphasising their respective gods’ divine bodies.
In The Eunuch, first performed in 161 BCE, the Roman comic playwright Terence (c. 190 BCE-c. 160 BCE) included a famous adage:
Sine Cerere et Baccho friget Venus, or without
Ceres and Bacchus, Venus freezes.
1
In other words, without food and wine, love grows cold. Thanks to the Tuscan humanist poet Petrarch (1304-1374), who produced a manuscript edition of Terence’s plays, and the first printed edition published in Venice around 1476 this proverb remained in popular use in Europe. Erasmus highlighted the adage in his compendium
Adagia, first published in Paris in 1500 and republished in an enlarged edition in Venice in 1508 as
Adagiorum chiliades tres.
2
Italian Renaissance painters, including Luca Signorelli (1450-1523), Titian (1488-1576), and Paolo Veronese (1528-1588) were the first to visualise the subject.
3
Later several sixteenth-century emblem books published in Northern Europe, included
Sine Cerere et Baccho friget Venus with small illustrations.
4
In these early images the emphasis tends to be either on the three Gods coming together to replenish love or a more moralising interpretation in which food and wine are kept happily at bay.
The motif of the enfeebled or “chilled” Venus, sometimes in variants where Ceres and Bacchus have already succeeded in restoring her warmth, emerged as a recurrent theme in the late 1580s, when several prominent Northern artists, most notably Bartholomeus Spranger (1546-1611) and Hendrick Goltzius (1558-1617), established it as a cornerstone of erotic imagery. Spranger, who served as court painter to the art-collecting Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II (1552-1612), produced around 1590 the canvas upon which the present ivory is based. In this work, he privileges the departure of Bacchus and Ceres, relegating Venus and Cupid to the background, where they are shown endeavouring to resist the cold.
5
Around 1597 Jan Harmensz. Muller (1571-1628) published a popular engraved version of Spranger’s painting which was reissued some years later with the figure of Venus omitted entirely to put the attention on Spranger’s elegant composition of Bacchus and Ceres.
6

catalogue_note:
Two other versions of this striking enamelled portrait exist: one in the Louvre and another in grisaille formerly in the collection of Yves Saint-Laurent and Pierre Bergé.
1
The present plaque is documented as early as 1866 when its previous owner Edward Greaves, a noted British collector of Limoges enamel, first brought it to a meeting at the Archaeological Institute in London.
After a career as a banker in Warwickshire, Edward Greaves (1803-1879) was M.P. for Warwick between 1852 and 1865 and again between 1874. He divided his time between London, Avonside, and Glen Etive in Western Scotland. Like many of his peers he was active in such societies as the Archaeological Institute in London and the Warwickshire Natural History and Archaeological Society, where occasionally he exhibited items from his extensive collection, including the present tondo. Objects from his possession were also lent to some of the large public exhibitions of the time, including the
National Exhibition of Works of Art at Leeds of 1868, where he contributed boxwood sculpture, cutlery, snuff boxes and twenty-five painted enamels. His two-part sale at Christie, Manson and Woods on 22 and 23 April 1874, which was apparently organised on the occasion of his retirement to Scotland, shows he was an astute collector of silver and pottery but was particularly well-versed in painted Limoges enamels. Greaves’ sale contained eighty examples of mainly signed Limoges enamels which had been acquired from some of the greatest works of art collections that came to auction in his lifetime, such as Walpole (1842), Bernal (1845), and Soltykoff (1861).
Lodewijk Benjamin de Hoop (1903-2002) was the director of A. de Hoop N.V., an electrotechnical company in Rotterdam founded by his father and uncle. He became director at age 27 and led the company through difficult times, including World War II, during which he was briefly imprisoned and his company was placed under German control. After the war, despite initially considering selling the business, he rebuilt it and led it until its sale in 1965. With the financial means and interest in art, De Hoop began collecting antiques at a young age, possibly influenced by his uncle and later guided by the antiquarian Jaap Wiegersma. Their friendship, which started after 1945, greatly shaped De Hoop's collection, particularly through shared travels and acquisitions in France and Italy. The collection reflects Wiegersma's taste, with a focus on medieval ivory, Limoges enamel, sculptures, Chinese artifacts, and Renaissance weapons. After Wiegersma’s death in 1967, De Hoop continued acquiring art through dealers and auctions. His collection, later inherited by his daughters and grandchildren, continued to grow until the 1980s and remains a testament to his passion and friendship with Wiegersma.

catalogue_note:
Whereas most wooden crosses from Mount Athos were set in filigree mounts, the present example has been fitted with a solid silver stand of extraordinary architectural refinement. The silver has been carefully but confidently smithed in a succession of complex forms and delicate patterns without ever overpowering the cross inside.
The base, the footprint of which follows a shape typical of early Baroque architecture, is stepped and interspersed first with a frieze with three-dimensional cherubs and foliate decoration that has been carefully worked open to form an ajourée relief and secondly with an engraved floral border. The stem of the cross is balanced atop the dragon’s head which is so often a feature of orthodox liturgical works of art, including episcopal staffs and katzis. From the serpent’s open mouth streams fine scrollwork, which supports a set of four stylised palm leaves. Immediately under the cross is a stepped baluster with twisted wire edges and minute foliate engravings on its concave shaft. Each of the cross terminals is an architectural dome such as those found on orthodox church buildings and their replicas. Each rests on four columns with acacia-leaf capitals and house a smiling cherub. From silver petals atop the domes springs a pistil of precious coral beads and seed pearls, each fixed into place by a twisted gilt silver wire. Each scene on the wooden cross is framed by pair of twisting columns which supports an arch. From top to bottom the arches are made up of miniature Rococo scrollwork, whilst from left to right there is a double arch: the lower lined with a string of exceedingly small pearls and the upper with engraved lines and a scallop shape on top. Each architectural compartment is punctuated by seed pearls in the corners. Adorning the edges of the cross are four foliate volutes at the base crowned by two emerald glass pastes. Eight more smiling cherubs with a single leaf above their heads sit atop scrollwork in the corners of the cross arms. Behind these cherubs further ensembles of coral beads and seed pearls were placed. The wooden cross that is on display in this wondrous work of silversmithing is itself especially fine.
Each side has six scenes from the lives of the Virgin and Christ, carefully carved into circular or oval registers with much openwork and depth. Represented from top to bottom and from left to right are the
Annunciation, the
Presentation in the Temple, the
Baptism of Christ,
Presentation of the Virgin,
Nativity of the Virgin, and the
Koimesis on one side and the
Crucifixion,
Raising of Lazarus,
Lamentation, the
Incredulity of Thomas,
Entry into Jerusalem, and
Anastasis on the other.

catalogue_note:
Benefiting from its geographical location at the heart of the Mediterranean, the city of Trapani, on the western coast of Sicily, was one of Europe’s leading commercial ports in the 17th and 18th centuries. By exploiting its natural resources, notably the extensive coral reefs off its coast, it also distinguished itself through the production of sumptuous objects, both for daily use and for religious devotion, combining coral with gilded copper, in some cases partially enamelled. Trapani’s production reached its peak between 1628, when the coral-workers’ guild was founded, and 1672, with the suppression of the uprising and the dispersal of the guild’s artisans. Highly prized for its colour, distinctive texture and rarity, coral has also been sought after since antiquity for its prophylactic properties.
According to handwritten notes on a note card belonging to Monsignor Giuseppe Pescini (1875 - 1950), who was summoned to the Vatican by Pius X on 12 August 1903, this plaque is said to have been donated by the Holy Father for the charity raffle in benefit of St Bartholomew’s Church.

catalogue_note:
In 1624, whilst a plague epidemic was raging in Sicily, Saint Rosalie is said to have appeared on several occasions to reveal the location of her relics on Mount Pellegrino. The epidemic came to an end on 15 July 1625, exactly one year to the day after the discovery of the relics. Rosalie was then proclaimed the patron saint of Palermo, and depictions of her became increasingly common there from that date onwards. The roses, which the two angels are shown holding in baskets here, are among the saint’s attributes, alongside the lily, symbolising her virginity.
Another shrine of a similar style, depicting Saint Rosalie flanked by Saint Joseph and Saint Michael, can be found at the Victoria and Albert Museum (inv. M.157-1956); another, depicting the Virgin surrounded by Saint Bruno and Saint Rosalie, was recorded in the 1960s at Beloeil Castle (Belgium), in the collections of the Princes of Ligne (see A. Dameu, op. cit., no. 25 and fig. 2b).

Prized for the fineness of its cutting and the precision of its engraving, rock crystal became increasingly popular during the Renaissance for the production of sumptuous functional objects and jewellery. In Milan, during the 1560s and 1570s, precious marten or sable heads were carved in rock crystal, mounted in gold and adorned with gemstones, then sewn onto the ends of furs worn around the neck or arm, or tucked into a belt (see Musée national de la Renaissance, Château d’Écouen, inv. Ec. 2109, and the Thyssen-Bornemisza Collection, Madrid, inv. DEC 0731). The Milanese workshops of the Miseroni and Sarracchi families were particularly renowned for their work in rock crystal.
Small crosses intended for private devotion, similar to the present example, also became increasingly widespread during this period. They were mounted in gold, sometimes enamelled, and embellished with pearls and precious stones. A comparable cross, hollowed out to form small cavities containing relics, is in the Victoria & Albert Museum (inv. 330-1864).

catalogue_note:
Hans Jakob Mair, a Celebrated Goldsmith in his Time
Hans Jakob Mair registered his hallmark in Augsburg in 1641 and played an influential role in the guild, serving as a council member from 1679 to 1682 and then as director from 1684 to 1686. His production is varied, encompassing large presentation dishes characteristic of Augsburg, with contoured rims and centres embossed with mythological or ancient scenes, as well as tankards and cups. He is best known for his pieces combining silver, gilt silver, hardstones, and colored enamels. During the Renaissance and throughout the 17th century, princes and wealthy collectors created cabinets of curiosities, displaying objects made of diverse, exotic materials or in original shapes. Silver-gilt pieces may thus be paired with nautiluses, turbo shells, coconuts, or ivory. Mair specialised in caskets with hardstone plaques, such as jasper, rock crystal, or, in our case, bloodstone. The mounts are in silver-gilt, decorated with extensive coloured enamel decoration. These objects were not intended for practical use but rather to display the wealth and taste of their owner. Mair’s creations are renowned throughout Europe and can be found in various museums today.
In 1675, he delivered a rock crystal, gold, turquoise, and enamel ewer to Leopold I, Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire, who gave it to Tsar Alexis Mikhailovich (Kremlin Museum, inv. M3-1270).
Similarly, a monstrance decorated with blue and red enamels, dated to 1668, is preserved at the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, alongside a rock crystal ewer (inv. 2369) and a table clock, circa 1665–1669 (inv. 1119). Each piece showcases his signature enamel work in white, red, green, and blue, with leafy scrolls and flowers.
A magnificent gilt silver, rock crystal, and enamel casket, dated to 1663, was sold at Sotheby’s Paris, Hôtel Lambert,
Une Collection Princière, vol. II, Kunstkammer, October 12, 2023, lot 273. It came from the collections of the German branch of the Rothschild family, whose members sought to recreate cabinets of curiosities in their homes, amassing the finest Renaissance pieces and recognizing the quality of Mair’s work.
The Art of Enamel, a Princely Taste
The combination of precious materials and enamel dates back to the Middle Ages, notably with the technique of enamel on gold, a Parisian speciality around 1400. It is not until the mid-17th century that the most imposing, astonishing, and fantastical pieces, paired with hardstones, are created. Thus, cups made of various stones (agate, jasper, amber, lapis, sardonyx, rock crystal, etc.), from ancient or contemporary times, are paired with mounts in silver, silver-gilt, or gold, enhanced with painted enamels. This technique became a speciality of several cities, such as Milan and Prague with the Miseroni workshops, and Paris. Cardinal Mazarin and King Louis XIV assembled exceptional collections, now preserved at the Louvre Museum.
In Germany, the centres of Nuremberg and Augsburg drew inspiration from French pieces and the Miseroni workshops to create objects appealing to the various princes of German cities. Mair crafted a magnificent casket with a simple use of blood jasper plaques, contrasted by an exuberant decoration of flowers and scrolling foliage in various colors. The most striking feature is undoubtedly the finial in the form of Cronos holding a child in his left arm, rendered realistically with various colored enamels.
It is all the more significant because this finial is crafted in gold with the application of enamels using the 15th-century Parisian technique. This technique is renowned as the most challenging to produce due to the differences in temperature and the high costs involved. Mair is thus an exceptional goldsmith who may have found inspiration by admiring the Golden Horse, one of the finest pieces of gold enameled work, preserved at the Collegiate Church of Saint Philip and Saint James in Altötting, near Munich, attributed to a Parisian workshop. A gift from Queen Isabeau of Bavaria to her husband, King Charles VI of France, in 1405, this piece was pawned by the king to his brother-in-law, Duke Louis of Bavaria, and has been in Bavaria since that time.
The depiction of this mythological figure is not coincidental. Cronos, the master of the gods, following an oracle, devours all his male children to avoid losing his power but is ultimately killed by his son Zeus. This image reflects the symbolism of the fragility of power, suggesting that one should not seek to preserve it at all costs. A true humanist prince must remain an enlightened, open, and curious man, rather than a mere despot.

catalogue_note:
The present relief portrays the poignant scene of Christ’s entombment. Joseph of Arimathea supports Christ’s head, while Nicodemus attends to His feet. At the centre, the Virgin Mary gazes sorrowfully over her son’s lifeless body, and in the foreground Mary Magdalene leans mournfully against the stone slab, her ointment jar resting beside her.
This tableau, along with other scenes from the Passion of Christ, were popular subjects for English alabaster reliefs of the 14th and 15th centuries, though individual depictions vary in their details. The present composition compares closely to a relief in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London (inv. no. A65-1946).

In the second half of the 15th century, Languedoc experienced a remarkable artistic revival, marking the end of a devastating trilogy of plague, war and famine. Following the conclusion of the Hundred Years’ War in 1453, and then the terrible fire of 1463, which destroyed nearly two-thirds of Toulouse, this commercial city, situated at the crossroads between the Kingdom of France and the Iberian Peninsula, returned to prosperity. A new generation of artists arrived, drawn by growing demand from influential families such as the Bourbon and Amboise, wealthy merchants, powerful members of the clergy and lawyers. They would become the driving force behind a genuine renaissance of the arts in Languedoc. Among the sculptors active in the region in the mid-15th century were Jacques Morel (1390–1459), from Lyon and influenced by Burgundian art, and his pupil Pierre Viguier, whose influence extended across Rodez, Montpellier and Toulouse. Between 1492 and 1495, a sculptor of Brabantine origin, the Brussels-born Pierre Brucy, also known as Bracin, is mentioned on several occasions in the Montpellier registers.
The present Virgin is fully representative of the fusion that took place during this period between influences from northern Europe and a vernacular style characteristic of late Gothic Languedoc, distinguished by elegant silhouettes, a pronounced taste for ornamental detail and exceptionally gentle facial features. The Virgin’s elongated oval face, narrow mouth, long, slender nose, high and perfectly arched eyebrows, almond-shaped eyes and pronounced eyelids are entirely consistent with the Brabantine style of the final quarter of the 15th century, dominated by the outstanding Borman dynasty. The delicate features of the present Virgin may be compared with those of an oak
Mary Magdalene, dating from around 1490–1500 and attributed to Jan I Borman (active circa 1460–1502) (Royal Museums of Art and History, Brussels, inv. 2992), as well as with the pose of an oak
Virgin and Child, dating from around 1460–1470 and attributed to the same sculptor (M-Leven, Leuven, inv. C/363), and another example dating from around 1510, attributed to Jan III (Musée du Louvre, inv. RF 43).
While the Brabantine influence is striking, certain elements reveal a more specifically Languedocian heritage, notably the Virgin’s broad curls, whose exaggeratedly sinuous curves recall the manner of the Master of Rieux. Formerly attributed to Jacques Morel,
Notre-Dame des Grâces
(or
Nostre Dame de Grasse) epitomises the exceptionally refined Toulouse sculpture of the final third of the 15th century (Musée des Augustins, Toulouse, inv. RA 788). Similarly, the meticulously rendered ornamental details on the present Virgin’s garments, such as the clasp fastening her mantle and the richly worked band securing her veil, translate into sculpture the splendour of Toulouse goldsmiths’ work. Its rich, partially preserved polychromy, meanwhile, is reminiscent of the vibrant colours of Languedocian illuminated manuscripts. Finally, a parallel may be drawn between the pose of the present Virgin and that of a Virgin in the church of Saint-Benoît at Bellegarde, in the Tarn. Although slightly later, dating from around 1510, the Bellegarde Virgin holds a raised fold of her mantle in the same manner, tucked beneath her right forearm. Two similar, long, flowing locks frame her face, while an abundance of ornamental details—including the mantle clasp, the richly decorated band adorning her head, and the rosary from which medals and a branch of coral are suspended—reveals a comparable fascination with precious detail.
First documented around 1930 in the collection of the Reverend Father Daniel Belbèze, prior of the Carmelite monastery in Rennes, who had recently acquired the Hôtellerie Sainte-Foy in Moissac, the present Virgin subsequently passed into the hands of Dr Hulin, a physician with a keen interest in the history, archaeology and heritage of the Périgord region. After exhibiting part of his collections at the Château de Reignac, he opened his Musée du Rempart in Sarlat, housed in the Tour du Bourreau. Following his death, the collection was dispersed in Paris on 12 December 1966. The present Virgin was then described as a Languedocian work dating from the late 15th or early 16th century and compared with works attributed to Pierre Brucy. When the sculpture was subsequently published by Jacqueline Boccador and Édouard Bresset, the authors confirmed its Languedocian origin and late 15th century date, but did not retain the attribution to this sculptor, of whose actual output very few works are known.

description_en:
Eastern France, probably Northern Burgundy, circa 1400

limestone, so-called 'pierre de Tonnerre'; on a wooden base by Kichizo Inagaki
inscribed: SN in red on the neck

catalogue_note:
International Gothic emerged from a new artistic flowering that began towards the end of the Hundred Years’ War. It developed in Western Europe, where intense diplomatic, familial and cultural relations were forged, and was shaped by the movement of architects, painters and sculptors from one court to another in search of new patrons. The result was a shared artistic language, tinged with certain regional characteristics. This imposing head, possibly representing Saint Peter and originating from an independent statue or an apostolic series that has since been lost, bears witness to this blending of influences.
The sinuous locks of the hair and beard, composed of alternating broad curls and tightly coiled strands, together with the expressive intensity of the facial features, point to the influence of sculpture from the Upper Rhine region. Comparisons may be drawn with statues of an
Emperor and a
Cleric, originating from the octagon of the spire of Strasbourg Cathedral, circa 1400–1410. Although now severely damaged, their original appearance is known through 19th century casts (circa 1400–1410; see
Strasbourg 1400, op. cit., pp. 118–123). The forelock, which stands out distinctly at the top of the forehead, the gaunt cheeks with their prominent cheekbones, and the broad curls of the hair are also comparable to a figure of
Saint Paul, another example of Strasbourg sculpture, dating from circa 1390 (Musée de l’Œuvre Notre-Dame, Strasbourg, inv. MOND 301). The expressiveness of the face, with its almost caricatural features, also recalls the
Saint Peter from the
Fischmarktbrunnen
(Fish Market Fountain) in Basel, dating to the 1380s (Historical Museum, Basel; see
Strasbourg 1400, op. cit., p. 122, fig. 4).
However, whereas Upper Rhenish sculpture is distinguished by the almost exclusive use of sandstone, examination of the limestone from which the present head was carved indicates that it originated in ancient quarries in northern Burgundy, between the banks of the Yonne south of Auxerre and the area around Tonnerre. Its composition may also be compared with that of Normandy chalk. As the stone used for the present work is harder and denser than chalk, however, this second hypothesis seems unlikely. During the Middle Ages, this type of limestone, known as “pierre de Tonnerre”, was widely used in Burgundy, between Auxerre and Dijon, as well as in southern Champagne, around Troyes.
Indeed, the naturalistic treatment of the facial features and the meticulous attention to detail, such as the numerous wrinkles crossing the forehead and accentuating the corners of the eyelids, also point towards Burgundy in the final decades of the 14th century, in the circle of Jean de Marville, Claus Sluter and Claus de Werve, the great master sculptors responsible for the Chartreuse de Champmol. The verticality of the elongated, gaunt face of our
Head of a Bearded Man may thus be compared with that of the fragmentary Christ from Sluter’s
Crucifixion, circa 1395–1399, which once surmounted the
Well of Moses
(Musée archéologique, Dijon, inv. Arb. 1323). Also comparable is the realism of the faces of the elderly men represented as
Prophets around the base of the well, their features weathered by time. These are emblematic of a shared cultural and artistic milieu.
A further comparison may be made with a
Head of an Apostle dating from the late 14th century, originating from the chapel of the Château de Mehun-sur-Yèvre, property of Jean de Berry, where the building campaign was entrusted to André Beauneveu (see
Le faste du gothique, op. cit., p. 155, no. 105; Louvre Museum, inv. RF 1979). The familial ties between the neighbouring duchies of Berry and Burgundy were also reflected in the artistic sphere. We know, moreover, that in 1393 Philip the Bold sent Claus Sluter and the painter Jean de Beaumetz to Berry, to study the prestigious project being undertaken for his brother, and to draw the lessons necessary to fulfil his own ambitions.
Another distinctive feature of our
Head of a Bearded Man is its wooden base by Kichizō Inagaki (1876–1951), which helps document the work’s modern history. A graduate of the Tokyo School of Fine Arts, Inagaki settled in Paris in July 1906. There, he revolutionised the conventions of framing and mounting through his seemingly minimalist approach to woodworking and his pared-back forms. He collaborated with dealers in non-Western art Paul Guillaume and Charles Ratton, as well as with Auguste Rodin, principally between 1912 and 1916, having met the sculptor through the antiquarian Joseph Brummer. In particular, he made frames for Egyptian reliefs that Rodin had acquired from Brummer (Musée Rodin, inv. Co.01040, Co.01050, Co.01051 and Co.03483). Joseph Altounian, who had discovered in Cairo some of the works that Brummer subsequently sold to Rodin, was also part of this select circle and almost certainly came into contact with Inagaki. The magnificent mount created by Inagaki for the present head, at an unknown date but certainly before 1951, indicates that the work most probably entered the Altounian collection during Joseph’s lifetime.
A report on the identification of the stone was provided by Annie and Philippe Blanc, doctors of geology, on 30 September 2026.

catalogue_note:
This majestic
Virgin and Child, much larger than the examples usually found on the art market, shows stricking similarities with other examples attributed to the Parisian workshops from the second quarter of the 14th century. The elongated silhouette and general posture of the Virgin, her face turned towards the Child, her body forming a slight contrapposto with her right leg bent, are comparable to the prototype of the
Virgin and Child of Bouée (Loire-Atlantique), and those of Lévis-Saint-Nom (Yvelines) and Tœufles (Somme). The perfectly oval shape of the Virgin’s face, the gentle softness of her features, the tall crown on her head (now missing its fleurons), her wavy hair flowing freely from beneath her veil, and the deep folds of her dress and cloak are all features characteristic of Parisian workshops.
Less common details on this example allow us to draw some more specific parallels. For example, the tender gesture of the Virgin's open right hand, on which the Child's left foot rests, can be found on two examples in the Val-d'Oise, in the parish churches of Ennery and Montigny-lès-Cormeilles. Similarly, the Child's right hand grasping one side of his mother's veil is a touching detail that can be found on an example of similar size in Prunay-sur-Essonne. We understand from the composition that the other side of the Virgin's veil, which seems to be pulled to the right instead of falling naturally, must also have been held by the Child's now missing left hand. This last detail is similar to the composition of the
Virgin and Child in Courtomer (Seine-et-Marne). Finally, all of these iconographic features can also be observed in the
Virgin and Child from the parish church of Labbeville (Val-d’Oise), where only the movement of the lower part of the Virgin’s body is reversed—making it the closest parallel to the present example.
In the first half of the 20th century, when the present
Virgin and Child belonged to the collection of the Kortrijk textile industrialist Louis de Poortere, it was thought to have originated from the former abbey of La Cour-Dieu. Although no conclusive evidence confirming this provenance has come to light, the hypothesis remains plausible.
The wealthy Cistercian abbey of Notre-Dame de La Cour-Dieu was founded in 1119 in the heart of the forest of Orléans. Placed under the protection of the kings of France and graced with visits from Saint Louis (1256), Charles IV the Fair (1322), and Philip VI (1342), it flourished until the late 14th century, before suffering successive waves of destruction during the Wars of Religion and later the Revolution. In 1791, the deconsecrated abbey and its contents—by then national property—were sold to Mr. Gentil, an unscrupulous speculator and leader of the so-called Bande Noire. Most of the buildings were demolished, and the stones resold. Sold again in 1793, the site underwent further devastation, marking the final dispersal of its movable heritage. The ruins of La Cour-Dieu later inspired Romantic artists before being partially rebuilt by Félix Desbois during the height of the Neo-Gothic revival. The estate subsequently changed hands several times, serving in turn as a farm and a motorcycle factory. The site was finally listed as a Historic Monument in 2012. Among the best-known masterpieces from La Cour-Dieu is the marble
Virgin and Child in the Musée des Beaux-Arts d’Orléans, attributed to André Beauneveu (c. 1335–1400) (inv. A.153; height 170 cm).
It is also worth noting that the library of Carlo de Poortere (1917–2002), son of Louis and a renowned bibliophile, was sold by Sotheby’s in Paris on 6 November 2014.

catalogue_note:
The earliest references to bird-shaped pyxides of this kind, evoking the dove of the Holy Spirit, are found in the writings of Tertullian, dating from the early 3rd century (see B. Drake Boehm, introduction to Chapter III C, in
Corpus des émaux méridionaux
[CD-ROM]). Originally made of gold or silver, these objects have rarely survived the successive campaigns of precious-metal melting. Very few examples remain, such as those from Saint-Yrieix in Limousin and the Silos Treasure. According to early texts, the Abbey of Grandmont, renowned for its celebrated champlevé enamel antependium, dismantled and sold as national property in 1791, owned one of these early gold doves, stolen in 1183 by Henry the Young King, son of Henry II Plantagenet ( ibid.).
At the beginning of the 13th century, Limousin workshops drew inspiration from the typology of these precious prototypes to develop a new generation of
Eucharistic doves, made of gilt copper to imitate gold and embellished with shimmering enamels, whose techniques they had mastered to a high degree. These distinctive pyxides were among the movable furnishings of the liturgy. Suspended above the altar by small chains, they could be raised and lowered using a pulley. This ingenious system served to extend the metaphor of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost but also, more practically, to keep the consecrated Host out of reach of rodents. In their original arrangement, the doves were surmounted by a canopy fitted with a crown, of which a few rare examples have survived (see Musée de Cluny, inv. Cl. 14027).
The present dove is one of the few known examples in this corpus, which probably constitutes the most original - for its naturalism - and desirable group of Limoges enamels.
Anatomy of a
Eucharistic Dove
The construction of the present example is entirely consistent with that of securely attributed examples in the corpus of 13th century Limousin champlevé enamels. The bird’s body consists of two embossed, engraved and gilt copper sheets, joined vertically and secured by soldering and rivets. A teardrop-shaped dorsal lid, hinged at one end, opens to reveal the compartment intended to hold the Host; it is secured when closed by a rivet with a domed head. Feathers are engraved across the dove’s body, becoming smaller around the beak and progressively larger towards the tail. A slight projection on the upper part of the beak indicates the cere, while the eyes are made of blue-black glass beads. The wings are applied and attached to the body by rivets. They lie flat against the body, with their tips crossing over the upper part of the tail. Their enamel decoration depicts down feathers towards the front, followed by flight feathers arranged in three bands. A simulated ornamental border, enamelled in turquoise and punctuated with blue-black glass beads, separates the two registers of the wings. The upper side of the tail is also enamelled, with a pattern of tail feathers, while the underside consists of an embossed gilt copper sheet engraved with the same feather motif as the rest of the body. The reserved areas surrounding the feathers on the wings and tail are embellished with a fine punched pattern.
On most known examples, as on the present dove, the legs and base—the most vulnerable components of the ensemble—are later replacements. They result from the repeated handling of these elaborately crafted pyxides during Eucharistic celebrations. However, a few examples have retained their original bases. Some take the form of a dish comparable to a gemellion
(see Nationalmuseet, Copenhagen, inv. 443), while others are surrounded by crenellated walls with small towers (see Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, inv. Bk 17205). Other bases, consisting of an enamelled disc with four projecting arms for suspension, appear in most cases to be later additions, probably dating from the late 19th century, as with the dove in the Metropolitan Museum of Art (inv. 17.190.344). This variant is found in particular among the Spitzer examples, suggesting that he may have been responsible for introducing it (see The Frances Lehman Art Center
1, Vassar College, Poughkeepsie, inv. 2017.4; and the former David-Weill and Paul Salmon collections, whereabout unknown).
On some examples, the wings are also movable. Mounted on hinges, they can be spread as those of a living dove would be. With a few rare exceptions, such as the example in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (inv. 49.1075), this naturalistic variant is found chiefly among examples identified as late productions and thus appears to be an indication of modern manufacture, intended to meet the demand of collectors in the late 19th century.
Selected Comparisons
The construction and decoration of each of the approximately fifty known doves differ from one another. Some have a relatively slender silhouette, with a small head atop a long neck, while others are more compact, with a larger breast. Colour combinations also vary, as do the shapes of the beaks, eyes and legs, where the latter are original. The position of the wings is not governed by a strict convention either: on some examples, they rest on either side of the body without touching, while on others they cross just above or over the upper part of the tail.
Although the variations are virtually endless, certain similarities can be identified, allowing more coherent groups to be distinguished. The vertical arrangement of the down feathers on the wings of the present dove, for instance, sets it apart from most other examples. It is nevertheless found on the doves in Santa Maria e San Claudio, Frassinoro, in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (inv. no. 49.1075), and in the previously mentioned Frances Lehman Art Center and former David-Weill collection. Likewise, its slender silhouette can be compared with that of two doves previously sold in New York: one from the Ernst Boehlen collection (Sotheby’s New York, 7 February 2025, lot 606), and another now in the Wyvern collection ( ibid., 8 February 2007, lot 418; see P. Williamson, pp. 140-141; inv. 0754). It also bears a resemblance to the aforementioned example from the former David-Weill collection.
With its more slender silhouette, slightly simplified decoration and particular proportions, the present dove appears to belong to the second generation of this peculiar type of pyxides, which also includes the examples in the Metropolitan Museum of Art (see above) and the Musée du Louvre (inv. OA 8104). Although the dating of the approximately fifty examples that make up this corpus of Limousin champlevé enamels has not been definitively established, the ornamental features of the earliest examples appear to be more elaborate. The dove in Amiens, generally regarded as the earliest, dating to around 1200 (Musée de Picardie, inv. MP 992-4-16), provides a case in point. Its wings feature two richly decorated ornamental bands, rather than the single band found here, embellished with cabochons: one separates the down feathers from the first row of flight feathers, while the other marks the boundary of the second row. The earliest examples also appear to have a more compact silhouette, as seen once again in the Amiens dove, as well as in those in Baltimore (Walters Art Museum, inv. 44.77) and in the former Robert von Hirsch collection (his sale, Sotheby’s London, 22 June 1978, lot 239), the latter originating from the collegiate church of Notre-Dame in Erfurt (Thuringia).
Apparently unrelated to any chronological pattern, the various examples also differ in the number of colours applied within each enamel cell. These variations nevertheless make it possible to identify those examples that demonstrate the highest level of technical mastery in enamelling. On the present dove, for instance, three colours alternate across the flight feathers, while as many as four are used on the slightly broader down feathers, placing it among the most technically sophisticated examples.
Based on our current knowledge, the present
Dove was first documented in February 1911, when it appeared as lot 2569 in the landmark sale of the library and art collection of Robert Hoe III (1839–1909). An eminent American industrialist, bibliophile, and collector, Hoe headed R. Hoe & Co., one of the country’s leading printing-press manufacturers. A prominent philanthropist and influential figure in New York’s cultural life, he helped establish the Grolier Club in 1884, serving as its first president, and was among the founders of the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Following his death, his extensive collections were dispersed in auction sales held in 1911 and 1912. Works formerly in his possession are now held by major American institutions, including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Walters Art Museum, the Brooklyn Museum, and the Philadelphia Museum of Art.
At the 1911 sale, the
Dove was acquired by Yamanaka & Co., the influential art-dealing firm founded by Yamanaka Sadajirō (1866–1936). Having opened his first New York gallery in 1894, Yamanaka went on to establish branches in Boston, London, Paris, Beijing, and Chicago. The firm played a pivotal role in introducing Japanese, Chinese, and Korean art to Western collectors and museums, handling an extensive range of works, from Buddhist sculptures and Chinese porcelains to lacquerware, bronzes, paintings, and screens. Its distinguished American clientele included Charles Lang Freer and members of the Rockefeller family. The firm’s fortunes declined during the Second World War, when the US government seized its American assets in 1942; the remaining stock was subsequently dispersed in a series of auction sales, notably in 1944.
Preserved for at least three generations within a prominent Japanese family, the present
Dove was long misidentified as a Persian incense burner, despite its origins in the comparatively little-known tradition of medieval Western art. Yamanaka, who acquired several Japanese and Chinese bronzes at the Hoe sale, may have been responsible for this misattribution, which endured for more than a century. Its recent rediscovery thus represents a significant addition to the small corpus of Limoges champlevé enamels of this type, prized by collectors for both their rarity and their exceptional craftsmanship.
The results of the analysis of the copper alloy used for the dove’s body and of the enamel composition, conducted by portable X-ray fluorescence spectrometry (pXRF), are consistent with those obtained from other 12th and 13th century Limousin examples and reveal no markers of later production. An analytical report supplied by the CARAA laboratory, dated 7 October 2026, is available upon request.
We would like to thank Mr Erik Bijzet for kindly bringing to our attention the sale of the Robert Hoe III collection in February 1911, in which the present Eucharistic Dove was included.

catalogue_note:
Seated versions of the so-called
Vierge glorieuse, in which the Virgin is both crowned and censed by angels, are relatively rare on Gothic ivories and the configuration of the present left side of diptych seems to be unique. Only three diptych leaves seem to approach it: the Musée Dobrée in Nantes (inv. 969.7.38) and the Wernher collection in London (inv. 88259050) possess reliefs showing the censing angels on either side of the Virgin and a crowning angel descending from heaven whereas a relief in the Royal Fine Arts Museum of Brussels has all angels in the skies (inv. 2686).
1
French Gothic ivory diptych leaves, typically crafted in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, are exquisite examples of medieval religious art. These small, intricately carved panels were often hinged together to form diptychs used for private devotion. Made primarily from elephant ivory, the panels depict scenes from the life of Christ, the Virgin Mary, and various saints, serving as visual aids for meditation and prayer. Paris emerged as a major centre for ivory carving during this period, thanks to its access to luxury goods and skilled artisans. The city’s workshops were renowned for their refined Gothic style, marked by elegant figures, delicate drapery, and detailed architectural settings. These diptychs were typically owned by wealthy laypeople or members of the clergy, who used them to enhance their spiritual lives outside the formal church setting. Because of their portability, they allowed for devotion in domestic spaces or while traveling. The craftsmanship also reflected the owner’s social status and piety. Many of these works were made in series, with compositions replicated by workshops to meet demand. Today, French Gothic ivory diptychs are treasured in museum collections for both their religious significance and artistic mastery.
Lodewijk Benjamin de Hoop (1903–2002) was the director of A. de Hoop N.V., an electrotechnical company in Rotterdam founded by his father and uncle. He became director at age 27 and led the company through difficult times, including World War II, during which he was briefly imprisoned and his company was placed under German control. After the war, despite initially considering selling the business, he rebuilt it and led it until its sale in 1965. With the financial means and interest in art, De Hoop began collecting antiques at a young age, possibly influenced by his uncle and later guided by the antiquarian Jaap Wiegersma. Their friendship, which started after 1945, greatly shaped De Hoop's collection, particularly through shared travels and acquisitions in France and Italy. The collection reflects Wiegersma's taste, with a focus on medieval ivory, Limoges enamel, sculptures, Chinese artifacts, and Renaissance weapons. After Wiegersma’s death in 1967, De Hoop continued acquiring art through dealers and auctions. His collection, later inherited by his daughters and grandchildren, continued to grow until the 1980s and remains a testament to his passion and friendship with Wiegersma.

catalogue_note:
This spectacularly intricately made pendant consists entirely of fine gold filigree and beads, fashioned into a three-dimensional star with flowers at its points. Several comparable stars were found with jewellery hoards from Umayyad Spain, including a single, virtually identical star in gold in the Victoria and Albert Museum that was found together with dirhams from the rule of Al-Hakam II (961–76) and Hisham II (976–1008) in an earthenware jar in Lorca, Murcia in the late 19th century.
1
The Walters Art Gallery keeps six golden stars are part in a particularly abundant hoard found at the Umayyad royal residence Madinat al-Zahra outside Cordoba, which was destroyed in 1021.
2
Each of these stars consists of two outlines in twisted gold wire fused atop one another using an undulating flattened strip of gold. The corners and points of the stars are punctuated with beads, while the voids are filled with bead- or filigree patterns, in this case a heart-shaped floral element. As Jenkins observed, such patterns were clearly derived from Fatimid sources but are generally unique to the Umayyad Caliphate.
3
The Umayyad Caliphate in medieval Spain, also known as Al-Andalus, was established in 756 when Abd al-Rahman I, a member of the Umayyad dynasty who had escaped the Abbasid overthrow in Damascus, declared himself Emir of Córdoba. This marked the beginning of a flourishing Islamic state in the Iberian Peninsula, which became a center of culture, science, and learning. In 929 CE, Abd al-Rahman III elevated the status of the emirate to a caliphate, asserting independence from both the Abbasid and Fatimid caliphs and ushering in a golden age of prosperity and relative stability. One of the most notable aspects of Umayyad rule in Spain was their policy of religious tolerance: while Islam was the dominant religion, Christians and Jews were allowed to practice their faiths, live in their own communities, and participate in public life as dhimmis, or protected people. This atmosphere of coexistence, especially in cities like Córdoba, led to rich cultural exchanges and advancements in philosophy, medicine, and architecture. The caliphate lasted until 1031, when internal strife led to its fragmentation into smaller taifa kingdoms, but its legacy of intellectual and religious pluralism profoundly influenced medieval Europe.
